大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

source.title: 江城子·乙卯正月二十日夜记梦
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。

translation:
Ten years between the living and the dead—
all vast and dim. Though I do not try to recall,
forgetting is impossible.
Her lonely grave lies a thousand miles away,
and I have nowhere to speak this desolation.
Even if we met again, she might not know me:
my face dust-covered, my temples white as frost.

Last night, in a shadowed dream, I suddenly returned home.
By the small window, she was arranging her hair,
applying her rouge. We gazed at each other—
not a word, only a thousand rows of tears.
I know where my heart breaks, year after year:
a bright moonlit night, a hill of short pines.

source.title: 念奴娇·赤壁怀古
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

The Great River rolls east, its waves sweeping away a thousand ages of heroes.
West of the old fortress, they say, lies Red Cliff where Zhou Yu of the Three Kingdoms made his stand.

This world is but a dream—I pour one more libation to the river moon.

source.title: 江城子·乙卯正月二十日夜记梦
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。

source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。

source.title: 念奴娇·赤壁怀古
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

The Great River flows eastward,
Its waves have washed away
All the gallant heroes of a thousand ages.
West of the old fortress,
They say this is Red Cliff
Where Zhou Yu of the Three Kingdoms made his stand.

Jagged rocks pierce the sky,
Thundering waves crash the shore,
Rolling up a thousand heaps of snow.
The land and water are like a painting—
How many heroes in that age!

I think back to Gongjin in those days,
Xiao Qiao newly wed,
His heroic grace radiant.

My too-sensitive heart should make them laugh—
My hair has turned white so soon.
Life on earth is but a dream;
I raise a cup to the moon upon the river.

source.title: 念奴娇·赤壁怀古
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

The Great River surges east—
its waves have scoured clean
every hero of a thousand ages.
West of the old ramparts,
they say, is Red Cliff,
where Zhou Yu of the Three Kingdoms stood.
Jagged boulders spear the sky,
startling breakers pound the shore,
churning a thousand heaps of snow.
Land and river, painted whole—
how many great men graced a single age!

Far off, I dream of Gongjin in those days:
Little Qiao newly his bride,
his bearing fierce and fine.
Feather fan, silk cap,
laughing, chatting—
and masts and oars turned to ash and smoke.
My soul revisits that lost kingdom;
how the sentimental would laugh at me,
my hair already silvered.
Life is but a dream—
I raise a cup and pour it for the river moon.

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

translation:
By the Xunyang River at night I saw a friend depart,
Maple leaves and reed flowers trembled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, my guest stood by his boat;
We raised our cups but had no music to drink to.
Drunken yet joyless, bitter at the parting—
At parting, the wide river drowned the moon in its depths.
Suddenly a pipa sounded on the water;
I forgot to return, and he forgot to sail.
Following the notes, I asked who played;
The pipa fell silent, as if she meant to speak but held back.
I drew my boat close and invited her out,
Refilled the wine, trimmed the lamp, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls a hundred summons she came,
Still cradling her pipa, half-hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked two, three strings—
Before a melody formed, feeling was already there.
Each string muffled, each note full of thought,
As if telling of a life of thwarted ambition.
She lowered her brow and played on by instinct,
Spilling out all the endless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow twirling, sweeping then plucking—
First the Rainbow Robe, then the Six Strings.
The thick strings thundered like sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Thunder and whisper tangled together,
Large pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Birdsong sliding smooth beneath blossoms,
Then a stream choking, hard to flow under ice.
The cold, the stagnant, the strings froze and died;
Frozen, blocked, the sound paused a moment.
A new hidden sorrow, a dark regret was born—
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
Then a silver bottle burst, water spraying;
Iron cavalry charged, swords and spears clashing.
The tune ended; she swept the pick across the strings,
One final chord of four like tearing silk.
East boats and west barges lay silent,
All that was seen: the autumn moon white on the river's heart.
She mused, set the pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her face.
She said: "I was a girl of the capital,
My home lived near the Xiama Ridge.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
My name was on the first register of the Teaching Academy.
When I finished playing, even the great masters bowed;
When I finished my makeup, even the fairest were jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to drape me with silk—
One song and I received countless bolts of red gauze.
Gold-headed hairpins shattered to keep the beat;
Crimson skirts were stained with spilt wine.
This year laughter, next year laughter;
Autumn moon and spring breeze passed without a thought.
My brother went to war, my auntie died;
The evenings came, the mornings went, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, cold and still; few horses came—
When I grew old I married a merchant's wife.
A merchant values profit, cares little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I guard our empty boat at the river mouth;
The moonlight circles the ship, the river water is cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dreamed of girlhood;
In the dream I wept, and my rouge tears ran red down my face."

I had heard the pipa and already sighed;
Hearing these words, I sighed again and again.
We are both driftness under the same wide sky—
Meeting here, what need to have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished, bedridden in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year long I hear no strings or pipes.
I live near the Pen River on low, damp ground,
Where yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights—
I often take wine and pour it out alone.
Is there no mountain song or village flute?
They are so rough and harsh they are painful to hear.
Tonight I heard your pipa's language—
It was like hearing immortal music; my ears were suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you I will compose the Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back down, and the strings grew urgent.
Mournful, unlike the earlier notes;
The whole company heard it again and covered their faces weeping.
Who in the room shed the most tears?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked.

message.content:
By the Xunyang River at night I saw a friend depart,
Maple leaves and reed flowers trembled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted, my guest stood by his boat;
We raised our cups but had no music to drink to.
Drunken yet joyless, bitter at the parting—
At parting, the wide river drowned the moon in its depths.
Suddenly a pipa sounded on the water;
I forgot to return, and he forgot to sail.
Following the notes, I asked who played;
The pipa fell silent, as if she meant to speak but held back.
I drew my boat close and invited her out,
Refilled the wine, trimmed the lamp, and reopened the feast.
After a thousand calls a hundred summons she came,
Still cradling her pipa, half-hiding her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked two, three strings—
Before a melody formed, feeling was already there.
Each string muffled, each note full of thought,
As if telling of a life of thwarted ambition.
She lowered her brow and played on by instinct,
Spilling out all the endless things within her heart.
Light pressing, slow twirling, sweeping then plucking—
First the Rainbow Robe, then the Six Strings.
The thick strings thundered like sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Thunder and whisper tangled together,
Large pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Birdsong sliding smooth beneath blossoms,
Then a stream choking, hard to flow under ice.
The cold, the stagnant, the strings froze and died;
Frozen, blocked, the sound paused a moment.
A new hidden sorrow, a dark regret was born—
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
Then a silver bottle burst, water spraying;
Iron cavalry charged, swords and spears clashing.
The tune ended; she swept the pick across the strings,
One final chord of four like tearing silk.
East boats and west barges lay silent,
All that was seen: the autumn moon white on the river's heart.
She mused, set the pick among the strings,
Straightened her clothes, rose, and composed her face.
She said: "I was a girl of the capital,
My home lived near the Xiama Ridge.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
My name was on the first register of the Teaching Academy.
When I finished playing, even the great masters bowed;
When I finished my makeup, even the fairest were jealous.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to drape me with silk—
One song and I received countless bolts of red gauze.
Gold-headed hairpins shattered to keep the beat;
Crimson skirts were stained with spilt wine.
This year laughter, next year laughter;
Autumn moon and spring breeze passed without a thought.
My brother went to war, my auntie died;
The evenings came, the mornings went, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, cold and still; few horses came—
When I grew old I married a merchant's wife.
A merchant values profit, cares little for parting;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I guard our empty boat at the river mouth;
The moonlight circles the ship, the river water is cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dreamed of girlhood;
In the dream I wept, and my rouge tears ran red down my face."

I had heard the pipa and already sighed;
Hearing these words, I sighed again and again.
We are both driftness under the same wide sky—
Meeting here, what need to have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished, bedridden in Xunyang city.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
All year long I hear no strings or pipes.
I live near the Pen River on low, damp ground,
Where yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos crying blood and apes wailing in grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moon nights—
I often take wine and pour it out alone.
Is there no mountain song or village flute?
They are so rough and harsh they are painful to hear.
Tonight I heard your pipa's language—
It was like hearing immortal music; my ears were suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you I will compose the Song of the Pipa.
Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
Then sat back down, and the strings grew urgent.
Mournful, unlike the earlier notes;
The whole company heard it again and covered their faces weeping.
Who in the room shed the most tears?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked.

translation:
# The Song of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River, on a night of farewell,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill.
I dismount; my guest remains aboard his boat,
We raise our cups, but no strings fill the air.
Drunk yet joyless, grief hangs heavy at parting—
The vast river swallows the moon in its reflection.

Then, from the water, a pipa's voice arrives—
I forget to return, my guest forgets to sail.
I follow the sound, asking softly, "Who plays?"
The pipa pauses, as if about to speak, then falls silent.
I move my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Pour more wine, trim the lamp, resume the feast.
After a thousand calls, at last she comes,
Still clutching her pipa, half hiding her face.

She turns the pegs, plucks a few strings—
Before the melody forms, feeling already speaks.
Each string restrained, each note full of thought,
As if telling a lifetime of unfulfilled ambition.
Head bowed, she plays with effortless grace,
Pouring out all the boundless things in her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then plucking—
First "Rainbow Garments," then "Six Strings of Joy."

The thick strings thunder like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like lovers' murmurs.
Thunder and whisper interweave,
Like pearls great and small falling into a jade dish.
Now clear as orioles singing through blossoms,
Now choked as a spring struggling beneath ice.
The cold stream seizes, the strings congeal,
And in the silence, a hidden sorrow is born—
At this moment, no sound surpasses all sound.

Then—like a silver bottle bursting, water erupting,
Like iron cavalry charging, swords clashing and ringing.
At the song's end, she draws the plectrum across the center,
Four strings strike once, like silk tearing apart.
East boats and west barges fall utterly silent—
Only the white autumn moon on the river's heart remains.

She lingers, puts down the plectrum, tucks it among the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises with a composed face.
"I was a girl of the capital," she begins,
"My home lay beneath Shrimp Mound Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name enrolled in the first rank of the Imperial Academy.
After each song, even the master players bowed;
When I finished my makeup, even the finest courtesans grew envious.
The young nobles of the Five Tombs bid for my favors,
For one song I received bolts of red silk beyond counting.
Gold-inlaid combs shattered keeping the beat,
Crimson skirts stained by spilled wine.
This year laughter, next year laughter—
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed uncounted.
My brother went to war, my aunt died,
Evening came, morning came, my beauty faded.
My door grew cold, horses rare,
Aging, I married a merchant's wife.
He values profit, not parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; I guard this empty boat at the river's mouth,
Moonlight circles the hull, the water bitter cold.
Late at night I dreamed of my girlhood's affairs,
Wept in sleep, my tears staining the paint on my face.

I had already sighed at the pipa's song;
Now these words weigh still heavier on my heart.
We are both exiles cast to the earth's end—
What need to have known each other before this meeting?

Since last year I left the imperial capital,
Banned and bedridden in this town of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, without music—
All year long, no strings or pipes are heard.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo encircle my home.
What do I hear here at dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons wailing in grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
More often than not I pour wine and drain it alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Hoarse and grating, they are unbearable to hear.
Tonight I hear your pipa speak—
Like celestial music, my ears are suddenly made clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more song;
For you, I shall compose this Ballad of the Pipa.

Moved by my words, she stands a long while,
Then sits, tightens the strings—the music grows urgent.
Mournful, not like the voice before;
Everyone in the room weeps anew, covering their faces.
Who among them weeps the most?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou—his blue robe is soaked.

Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill.
I dismount; my guest remains aboard his boat,
We raise our cups, but no strings fill the air.
Drunk yet joyless, grief hangs heavy at parting—
The vast river swallows the moon in its reflection.

Then, from the water, a pipa's voice arrives—
I forget to return, my guest forgets to sail.
I follow the sound, asking softly, "Who plays?"
The pipa pauses, as if about to speak, then falls silent.
I move my boat closer, inviting her to appear,
Pour more wine, trim the lamp, resume the feast.
After a thousand calls, at last she comes,
Still clutching her pipa, half hiding her face.

She turns the pegs, plucks a few strings—
Before the melody forms, feeling already speaks.
Each string restrained, each note full of thought,
As if telling a lifetime of unfulfilled ambition.
Head bowed, she plays with effortless grace,
Pouring out all the boundless things in her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping then plucking—
First "Rainbow Garments," then "Six Strings of Joy."

The thick strings thunder like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like lovers' murmurs.
Thunder and whisper interweave,
Like pearls great and small falling into a jade dish.

Now choked as a spring struggling beneath ice.

source.title: 永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古
source.author: 辛弃疾
source.text:
千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？

translation:
**Perpetual Joy · Meditating on the Past at Beigu Pavilion, Jingkou**

A thousand autumns in these rivers and hills—
where now is Sun Zhongmou, the hero
beyond all seeking?

Dance pavilions, song terraces,
all that grace and splendor
washed away by rain, scattered by wind.

Slanting sun over grass and trees,
an ordinary lane, a common street—
they say young Jì-nù once lived here.
Remember those years: iron horses, golden spears,
a breath that swallowed ten thousand miles like a tiger.

In Yuanjia, rash and hurried,
he sought to seal the mound at Langjūxū—
and won only a panicked glance northward.
Forty-three years: still in my gaze I keep
the beacon-fires along the road to Yangzhou.

Who can bear to look back?
Beneath the temple of Fó Lí,
crows feast on offerings, drums of the village shrine
beat out their hollow rhythm.

Who will ask—
as the old general Lián Pō,
can I still eat well enough
to ride again?

Eternal the rivers and mountains, yet where can we find
the heroes of old—Sun Zhongmou's daring, his might?

in common lanes and ordinary streets,
people still say Ji Nu once lived here.

a spirit that swallowed ten thousand li like a tiger's roar!

crows peck at offerings, drums and incense smoke
mingle in blind devotion.
Who now would ask, as of Lian Po grown old:
"Can you still eat? Can you still ride to war?"

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

translation:
# The Song of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River, on an autumn night, I saw off a guest;
maple leaves and reed blossoms trembled in the rustling wind.
I dismounted my horse; my friend sat aboard his boat—
we raised our cups to drink, yet no pipes or strings were near.
Drunken, we found no joy; grief hung over our parting;
at the moment of farewell, vast moonlight drowned the river.
Suddenly, over the water, a pipa's voice drifted in—
I forgot to go home; my guest forgot to sail.

We followed the sound, asking softly, "Who plays so?"
The pipa paused; she wished to speak yet lingered in silence.
I moved my boat closer and invited her to appear;
we poured fresh wine, trimmed the lamp, and reopened the feast.
A thousand calls, ten thousand summons—only then she came,
still holding her pipa, half-concealing her face.
She turned the pegs and plucked a few tentative strings;
before the melody formed, emotion had already spoken.
Each string was heavy with sigh; each note deep with thought—
as if telling of a lifetime's thwarted ambitions.
Eyes lowered, fingers moving with unhurried grace,
she poured out the endless sorrow within her heart.
Light sweeps, slow rolls, glides and plucks in turn—
first the *Rainbow Feather*, then the *Six Strings* followed.

The thick strings thundered like sudden rain in storms;
the thin strings whispered like lovers in secret talk.
Thundering, whispering, intertwined they rang—
great pearls, small pearls tumbling onto a jade plate.
Now the songbird's tongue, smooth beneath the flowers;
now a stifled spring, struggling beneath the ice.
The cold spring seizes; the strings freeze and stop—
the flow is choked, the sound falls silent for a moment.
Yet a hidden grief, a secret resentment stirs—
at this moment, silence surpasses sound.
Then a silver vase bursts, water jets forth;
iron cavalry charges, blades and spears clash.
The song ends: she draws the plectrum across the center—
one cry of four strings, like silk torn apart.

East boats, west barges—all fell mute;
only the autumn moon shone white upon the river's heart.
She paused, set the plectrum among the strings,
straightened her robes, and rose with composed dignity.
"I was born a girl of the capital," she spoke,
"my home near the Shrimp Mound, by the old terraces.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
my name was entered in the first division of the Teaching Bureau.
When my songs ended, even great masters bowed in awe;
when I made up my face, the fairest courtesans grew jealous.
The young lords of Five Tombs vied to offer me silk—
one song earned bolts of red gauze beyond counting.
Jeweled combs struck the beat until they shattered;
blood-red skirts were stained by spilling wine.
This year of laughter, next year of revelry—
autumn moons and spring breezes passed like idle hours.
Then my brother joined the army; my aunt died;
dusk came, dawn went, and my beauty faded.
My gate grew cold; horses and carriages came fewer.
When age crept in, I married a merchant's wife.
He prizes gold, not farewell—last month he sailed
to Fuliang for tea, leaving me at the river mouth.
He goes; I stay, guarding an empty boat—
moonlight circles me; the river water turns cold.
Deep in the night I dreamed of my youth's affairs;
in dreams I wept, my painted tears staining the rails."

I had heard the pipa and already sighed;
now, hearing her words, I sighed again and again.
We are both wanderers lost at heaven's edge—
if we meet, why must we have known each other before?
I left the imperial capital last year,
banished, bedridden, in this Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, with no music at all;
throughout the year, no silk or bamboo sounds reach my ears.
I live near the Pen River, where the land is low and damp;
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear here, from dawn to dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding their calls; apes crying in grief.
On spring nights amid flowers, on autumn moons above—
often I take my wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes?
They are harsh and grating, unbearable to hear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's speech,
it is as if celestial music has cleared my ears.
Do not refuse to sit and play once more—
for you, I will compose this *Song of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
then sat and tightened the strings; the music grew urgent.
Sorrowful, unlike the notes before—
the whole room heard again, and all pressed hands to weeping.
Who among us shed the most tears?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through.

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

# The Ballad of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River, I saw a guest off at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn's chill.
I dismounted; my guest was already on the boat.
We raised our cups, yet had no music for the drink.
Half-drunk, joyless, sorrowful we parted—
Parting into a vast river drowned in moonlight.

Then suddenly, from the water, a pipa's voice—
I forgot to go home, my guest forgot to leave.
Following the sound, I asked in hush: who plays?
The music paused, as if the player wished to speak but hesitated.
I moved my boat close and invited her to come;
We poured fresh wine, relit the lamps, and opened the feast anew.
After a thousand calls, ten thousand entreaties,
She emerged at last, still holding the pipa half before her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked a few strings—
Before the melody formed, feeling already lived.
Each string suffocated, each note a sigh,
As if telling of a life's fortune denied.
Brows lowered, fingers moving at will,
She poured forth all the boundless things within her heart.
Light gathers, slow twists, sweeps and plucks—
First the "Rainbow Robe," then the "Six Strings."

The thick strings thundered like a sudden downpour;
The thin strings whispered like a private murmur.
Thunder and whisper, interwoven, tangled—
Big pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles singing, smooth beneath the blossoms;
Like a spring choking, struggling under ice.
Ice-chilled, the spring grows sluggish, the strings freeze and die;
Frozen, blocked, the sound falls silent for a while.
Then another hidden sorrow, a buried resentment stirs—
At this moment, silence speaks louder than sound.

A silver vase suddenly bursts—water erupts!
Iron cavalry surges forth, blades and spears clash!
The song ends; she draws the plectrum across the strings—
All four sound at once, as if silk were torn.
East boats and west barges, all hushed and still;
Only the autumn moon, white at the river's heart, was seen.

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

translation:
# The Ballad of the Pipa

One autumn night I saw my guest off by the Xunyang shore,
where maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the cold.
I mounted down, my friend aboard, we raised our cups in vain—
no pipe nor string to grace the drink, no music for the strain.
Though drunk, no joy could warm our parting; grief hung heavy in the air,
and when we said farewell, the river spread beneath the moon, vast and bare.

Then, suddenly, above the water came the sound of pipa strings,
and I forgot to go, my guest forgot to leave. We paused, and listened—
tracing the notes into the dark, we asked who played. The music stilled;
a voice seemed poised to speak, yet hesitated, shy and still.
We moved our boats together, called for her to share our wine,
rekindled lamps, and laid out fresh the banquet once more fine.
Though we called a hundred times, she came out slow,
still cradling her pipa half before her face, her grace aglow.

She turned the pegs and plucked a few tentative strings—
before a melody took shape, emotion already sang.
Each note restrained, each tone a sigh, as if she poured her whole life out:
all thwarted dreams, all bitter years beneath the brow's quiet doubt.
Her eyes cast down, her fingers flew, and in that endless playing told
the boundless sorrows of a heart too long held cold.
She pressed, she twined, she swept, she plucked—first "Rainbow Skirt," then "Six Strings' Call,"
the great thick strings roaring like sudden rain, the thin ones whispering soft and small.
Loud and soft together mingling, like pearls both large and small
falling on a jade plate, bright and clear, one after another's call.
Then smooth as orioles threading through the blossoms' velvet shade,
then choked as spring water struggling beneath the ice's cold cascade.
The ice pressed hard, the strings grew stiff, the sound seemed lost in silence deep—
and in that silence, hidden grief and buried rage awoke to weep.
For at such moments, no sound speaks louder than the sound of sound.

Then, like a silver flask that bursts, its water spraying wide,
like iron cavalry that charges, blades and armor clashing side by side—
the song reached its end; she swept the plectrum down, and all four strings
rang out as one, a single cry, like silk being torn in two.
East boats and west boats fell utterly silent, not a word was spoken,
only the autumn moon above the river's heart, pale and white, unbroken.

She lingered, drew the plectrum from the strings, straightened her dress with care,
and set her face in solemn grace. Then, speaking, told us there:
"I was a girl of the capital once, my home near Shrimp Mound's base.
At thirteen I had mastered pipa, and my name was placed
in the First Troupe of the Teaching Office. When I had finished playing,
even the finest masters bowed. When I had done my makeup,
all the beauties envied me. The young lords of Five Tombs
vied to shower me with scarlet silk; for a single song
I'd gather bolts of brocade beyond all counting.
Jeweled combs snapped to the beat, and blood-red skirts were stained with wine.
Year after year of laughter passed, the autumn moon and spring breeze
spent as if they'd never end. But then my brother went to war,
my auntie died, and morning turned to evening, evening turned to more.
The gate grew cold, the horses thinned, and when my beauty faded,
I married a merchant who weighs his gold above my shade.
Last month he left for Fuliang to buy his tea and trade,
and I have kept this empty boat since, the river cold, the moon bright,
and in the deep of night I dream of girlhood's vanished light—
I weep in sleep, and tears run down through rouge across my face like rain."

I heard the pipa and sighed before; now hearing these words, I sigh again.
We are both souls adrift at the world's far edge, and what need had we to meet as friends?
Since last year I left the imperial capital, banished, sick, in Xunyang's town I lie.
This place is remote, without all music; all year long no string nor pipe sounds nigh.
My dwelling sits near the Pen River's low and damp expanse,
where yellow reeds and bitter bamboo ring my house in melancholy dance.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk? The cuckoo's bleeding cry,
the gibbons' howl beneath the moon. In spring's flower-lit morn, in autumn's moonlit night,
I fill my cup and drink alone, for who would share this plight?
Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes? Their croaking, creaking tones
are harsh to hear, yet tonight, your pipa's voice—
like heavenly music strikes my ears and makes them clear again.
Do not refuse to sit once more and play another strain;
for you I'll write this Ballad of the Pipa, set it down in words.

Moved by my plea, she stood a while, then sat and turned the strings to fast—
so desolate, so unlike what she played before, that all the hall
wept again and hid their faces. Who among us wept the most?
The Jiangzhou Prefect in his blue robe—his sleeves were soaked with tears.

source.text:

I stand, I lean upon the tower's height,
the wind a threadbare whisper at my face.
I gaze till spring-sorrow fills every horizon—
a dimness blooming at the edge of space.

raise cup to song—yet forced mirth tastes like none.

for her sake I have withered, and that is true.

source.title: 念奴娇·赤壁怀古
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

translation:
**Nian Nu Jiao · Meditation at the Red Cliff**
*Su Shi*

The great river surges eastward;
its waves have swept away
a thousand ages of dashing heroes.
West of the old ramparts—
they say this is the Red Cliff
where Zhou Lang of Three Kingdoms made his stand.

Jagged boulders pierce the sky,
startling breakers thunder on the shore,
churning a thousand mounds of snow.
The land and river, a painting set in stone—
how many heroes rose in one brief breath!

Far off, I picture Gongjin in his prime:
the young bride Xiao Qiao newly won,
his bearing fierce, his spirit ablaze.
A crane-feather fan, a scholar's silk band,
and between his laughter and his ease
the warships of the foe
blazed out to ash and smoke.

My soul still wanders that old land.
Sentimental hearts would surely laugh at me—
these temples silvered far too soon.
All the world is but a dream;
so I pour one cup
to the river, and the moon.

source.title: 念奴娇·赤壁怀古
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

translation:
The Great River surges eastward,
its waves have swept away
the brilliant of a thousand ages.
West of the old ramparts—
they say this is Red Cliff,
where young Zhou of the Three Kingdoms held his ground.
Jagged stones pierce the sky,
thunderous breakers pound the shore
and churn a thousand heaps of snow.
Land and river, a painting—
how many heroes in that single age!

Far back I summon Gongjin in his prime:
Xiao Qiao newly wed,
his bearing heroic, radiant.
Feather fan, silk headband—
laughing, chatting easily,
the enemy's masts to ash,
vanishing in smoke.
My spirit wanders that ancient land;
perhaps they'd mock my tender heart,
my hair gone silver far too soon.
This human world is all a dream—
so I pour out a cup
to the moon over the river.

source.title: 念奴娇·赤壁怀古
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

translation:
The great river surges east, its waves scouring clean
all the gallant souls of a thousand ages.
West of the old ramparts, they say,
stands the Red Cliff of Zhou Lang in the Three Kingdoms' day.
Jagged boulders thrust into the sky,
frightened breakers pound the shore,
rolling up a thousand heaps of snow.
Land and river, a painting—
how many heroes in a single age!

Far I recall Gongjin in those years,
Xiao Qiao newly wed, his bearing bold and radiant,
feather fan in hand, silk cap on head,
laughing, chatting—and masts and oars
turned to ash, vanished in smoke.
My spirit wanders that ancient land;
how this sentimental heart should laugh at me,
with silver hair come too soon.
The world below is but a dream—
I raise one cup and pour it to the river moon.

source.title: 念奴娇·赤壁怀古
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

translation:
**To the Tune of *Nian Nu Jiao*: Meditations on the Past at Red Cliff**

The great river surges east;
its waves have washed clean
a thousand ages of heroes,
all their wind and grace.

West of the old ramparts,
they say, is Red Cliff—
where Zhou Yu of the Three Kingdoms
held his ground.

Jagged rocks pierce the sky,
thundering tides batter the shore,
rolling up a thousand heaps of snow.
Rivers and mountains, a living scroll—
how many heroes in one brief age!

Far off I recall Gongjin in his prime,
Xiao Qiao newly wed,
his bearing fierce, his spirit ablaze.

Feather fan, silk headband—
between his laughter and idle talk,
the masts and oars of the foe
crumbled to ash and smoke.

My soul roams the ancient land;
the sentimental would laugh at me—
my temples already silvered.

The world is but a dream.
I raise one cup and pour it
to the moon on the river.

translation:
Butterfly Loves the Blossoms
*I Linger at the High Tower in the Thin Wind*

I lean upon the tower's edge, the breeze a silver thread,
And gaze to where the sky dissolves—spring sorrow rises, dim.
In mist and waning light the grass still holds its green;
I say nothing, at the railing—what soul knows my ache?

I meant to cast off all restraint and drink until I drown,
To face the wine, to raise a song—but joy forced tastes of dust.
My belt loosens, loosens, yet I would not tighten it;
For her I waste away, haggard, and do not regret.

— Liu Yong

source.title: 念奴娇·赤壁怀古
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

The Yangtze surges east, its waves erasing
all heroes of a thousand ages gone.

lies Red Cliff—Zhou of Three Kingdoms' stand.

slam the shore, whipping up a thousand heaps of snow.

how many greats this single age!

when Little Qiao had just become his bride,
his bearing fierce, his spirit ablaze.

my hair gone silver far too soon.
This world is but a dream—
one cup, I pour to the river moon.

source.title: 永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古
source.author: 辛弃疾
source.text:
千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？

translation:
Eternal Joy — Gazing from Beigu Pavilion at Jingkou, Remembering the Past

A thousand ages of rivers and mountains remain,
yet no hero like Sun Zhongmou can be found.
The dancing pavilions, the singing terraces—
all that grace and glory,
swept away by rain and wind.
In the slanting sun, among grass and trees,
in an ordinary lane, they say
young Ji-nu once made his home.
And one recalls those years:
golden halberds, iron steeds—
his spirit swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger.

How rashly Yuanjia's Emperor marched
to seal his name on Langjuxu,
and gained only a panicked glance northward.
Forty-three years have passed;
looking out, I still remember
the beacon fires along the road to Yangzhou.
Can I bear to look back?
Beneath the shrine of Weldi,
crows peck at offerings, village drums resound.
Who is left to ask,
as of old Lian Po:
"You are grown grey—can you still eat a meal,
and ride to war?"

Eternal Joy — Gazing at the Past from Beigu Pavilion, Jingkou

A thousand ages of rivers and hills;
no hero to seek where Sun Zhongmou once reigned.
Dancing terraces, singing platforms —
all grace and glory, swept by rain,
stripped bare by the wind.

Slanting sun on grass and trees,
common lanes, humble streets —
they say Jinu lived here.
Think of those years: golden halberds, iron steeds,
a spirit swallowing ten thousand *li* like a tiger.

The Yuanjia campaign, rash and unprepared —
to seal Langjuxu they dared,
and earned only a panicked, northward stare.
Forty-three years gone, yet in my gaze I still recall
the beacon-fires along the road to Yangzhou.

How can one bear to look back?
Beneath Fuli's temple, a roar of sacred crows
and the thud of village drums.
Who will come to ask, as once they asked of Lian Po —
"Though old, can he still eat? Can he still fight?"

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。

translation:
The Song of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River on an autumn night I saw a friend depart,
maple leaves and reed flowers rustling in the cold.
I dismounted; he stood aboard the boat.
We raised our cups to drink, yet no pipes or strings were near.
Drunk, we found no joy—parting grew bitter still,
and when we parted, the vast river drowned the moon.

Then, suddenly, from the water came a pipa's cry—
I forgot my home, my guest forgot to sail.
We followed the sound, asking softly who played,
but the music paused as if she meant to speak, then held her tongue.
We shifted boats to reach her, begged her to appear,
refilled the wine, trimmed the lamp, and opened the feast anew.
After a thousand calls, ten thousand pleas, at last she came,
still half-concealing her face behind the pipa's curve.

She turned the pegs, drew across the strings—three, four notes—
and before a melody formed, feeling had already spoken.
Each string a sigh, each note a grief,
as though telling a life of thwarted dreams.
Eyes lowered, fingers drifting free,
she poured out all the boundless ache within.
Light gatherings, slow twistings, sweeps and pluckings—
first the "Rainbow Robe," then the "Six Strings of Joy."

The great strings thundered, sharp as sudden rain;
the small strings whispered, soft as lovers' talk.
Loud and soft intertwined, a jostling of pearls—
big and small falling on a jade plate, scattering.
Then a warbler's trill, gliding smooth beneath blossoms;
then a choked brook, struggling under ice.
The frozen spring grew sluggish, strings grew still;
stillness sealed them, sound suspended.
A hidden sorrow, a nameless rage was born—
in that silence, more was said than any sound could say.

Then, like a silver vase shattering, water bursting forth;
like armored cavalry charging, blades and spears clashing.
The song ended; her pick swept once across the center strings—
four notes in unison, like silk torn in two.
East boats, west barges: not a word.
Only the autumn moon, white upon the river's heart.

She sat in thought, set the pick between the strings,
straightened her dress, rose, composed her face.
"I was a girl of the capital," she told us,
"my home beneath the Toad Tomb Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
my name entered the First Troupe of the Imperial Academy.
When I finished a piece, even great masters bowed;
when I made up my face, even the autumn beauties envied.
Young lords of the Five Tombs vied to tie red silk on me;
one song, and bolts of crimson gauze beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs were snapped keeping time,
blood-red skirts stained dark with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter,
autumn moons and spring breezes passed as though they meant nothing.
Then my brother joined the army, my auntie died,
evenings came and went, and beauty faded.
The gate grew cold, the horses sparse—
too old, I married a merchant's wife.
He prized profit, thought little of farewell;
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He leaves, and I guard an empty boat at the river's mouth;
moonlight circles the hull, the water runs bitter-cold.
Deep in the night I dream of girlhood days,
wake weeping, tears cutting red lines down my painted face."

I had sighed already at the pipa; hearing her words, I sighed again.
We are both souls cast to the world's far edge—
what need for former knowing in this meeting?
I, since last year, left the imperial capital,
demoted to illness in this Xunyang town.
Xunyang lies remote, without its music;
all year long, no silk strings or bamboo pipes are heard.
My dwelling near the Pen River sits low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo ring the house.
From dusk to dawn, what do I hear?
The blood-crying cuckoo, the apes' keening wail.
Spring rivers, flower-mornings, autumn moons, nights—
I take my wine and pour it, drinking alone.
Is there no hillside song, no village flute?
The croaking, the clatter—ear-splitting, unbearable.
But tonight I hear your pipa's tongue,
and as if hearing celestial music, my ears grow clear.
Do not refuse—sit again, play one more piece.
For you, I shall remake this Song of the Pipa.

Touched by my words, she stood a long while still,
then sat, drew the strings tighter, and the music quickened.
Sorrowful, unlike the earlier sound—
the whole room, hearing again, buried their faces and wept.
Who wept most of all among those seated?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through.

{"title": "琵琶行", "author": "白居易", "text": "浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}

{"translation": "The Song of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River on an autumn night I saw a friend depart,
maple leaves and reed flowers rustling in the cold.
I dismounted; he stood aboard the boat.
We raised our cups to drink, yet no pipes or strings were near.
Drunk, we found no joy—parting grew bitter still,
and when we parted, the vast river drowned the moon.

Then, suddenly, from the water came a pipa's cry—
I forgot my home, my guest forgot to sail.
We followed the sound, asking softly who played,
but the music paused as if she meant to speak, then held her tongue.
We shifted boats to reach her, begged her to appear,
refilled the wine, trimmed the lamp, and opened the feast anew.
After a thousand calls, ten thousand pleas, at last she came,
still half-concealing her face behind the pipa's curve.

She turned the pegs, drew across the strings—three, four notes—
and before a melody formed, feeling had already spoken.
Each string a sigh, each note a grief,
as though telling a life of thwarted dreams.
Eyes lowered, fingers drifting free,
she poured out all the boundless ache within.
Light gatherings, slow twistings, sweeps and pluckings—
first the "Rainbow Robe," then the "Six Strings of Joy."

The great strings thundered, sharp as sudden rain;
the small strings whispered, soft as lovers' talk.
Loud and soft intertwined, a jostling of pearls—
big and small falling on a jade plate, scattering.
Then a warbler's trill, gliding smooth beneath blossoms;
then a choked brook, struggling under ice.
The frozen spring grew sluggish, strings grew still;
stillness sealed them, sound suspended.
A hidden sorrow, a nameless rage was born—
in that silence, more was said than any sound could say.

Then, like a silver vase shattering, water bursting forth;
like armored cavalry charging, blades and spears clashing.
The song ended; her pick swept once across the center strings—
four notes in unison, like silk torn in two.
East boats, west barges: not a word.
Only the autumn moon, white upon the river's heart.

She sat in thought, set the pick between the strings,
straightened her dress, rose, composed her face.
"I was a girl of the capital," she told us,
"my home beneath the Toad Tomb Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
my name entered the First Troupe of the Imperial Academy.
When I finished a piece, even great masters bowed;
when I made up my face, even the autumn beauties envied.
Young lords of the Five Tombs vied to tie red silk on me;
one song, and bolts of crimson gauze beyond counting.
Gold-ornamented combs were snapped keeping time,
blood-red skirts stained dark with spilled wine.
Year after year of laughter,
autumn moons and spring breezes passed as though they meant nothing.
Then my brother joined the army, my auntie died,
evenings came and went, and beauty faded.
The gate grew cold, the horses sparse—
too old, I married a merchant's wife.
He prized profit, thought little of farewell;
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He leaves, and I guard an empty boat at the river's mouth;
moonlight circles the hull, the water runs bitter-cold.
Deep in the night I dream of girlhood days,
wake weeping, tears cutting red lines down my painted face."

I had sighed already at the pipa; hearing her words, I sighed again.
We are both souls cast to the world's far edge—
what need for former knowing in this meeting?
I, since last year, left the imperial capital,
demoted to illness in this Xunyang town.
Xunyang lies remote, without its music;
all year long, no silk strings or bamboo pipes are heard.
My dwelling near the Pen River sits low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo ring the house.
From dusk to dawn, what do I hear?
The blood-crying cuckoo, the apes' keening wail.
Spring rivers, flower-mornings, autumn moons, nights—
I take my wine and pour it, drinking alone.
Is there no hillside song, no village flute?
The croaking, the clatter—ear-splitting, unbearable.
But tonight I hear your pipa's tongue,
and as if hearing celestial music, my ears grow clear.
Do not refuse—sit again, play one more piece.
For you, I shall remake this Song of the Pipa.

Touched by my words, she stood a long while still,
then sat, drew the strings tighter, and the music quickened.
Sorrowful, unlike the earlier sound—
the whole room, hearing again, buried their faces and wept.
Who wept most of all among those seated?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."}

source.text:
千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？

translation:
Eternal are the rivers, eternal the hills—
yet where, oh where, is Sun Zhongmou, the hero gone?
Dance pavilions, song terraces, all their grace
swept by rain, by wind, into the dust.

Slanting sun on grass and trees,
ordinary lanes, common alleys—
they say Ji Nu once dwelt here.
Think of those years: golden halberds, iron steeds,
a spirit that swallowed ten thousand leagues like a tiger.

Yuanjia's rash war-cry—
to raise the mound at Langjuxu—
bought only panicked glances north.
Forty-three years: in my sight I still recall
beacon fires along the road to Yangzhou.

How bear to look back?
Beneath the shrine of Fulan,
a clamor of sacred crows, the village drums.
Who will ask: Is Lian Po old,
and can he still eat his fill?

source.author: 柳永
source.text:
伫倚危楼风细细，望极春愁，黯黯生天际。
草色烟光残照里，无言谁会凭阑意。
拟把疏狂图一醉，对酒当歌，强乐还无味。
衣带渐宽终不悔，为伊消得人憔悴。

translation:
Butterflies Love the Flowers

I lean long upon the high tower, the breeze so fine,
gaze stretching to the farthest reach of spring—
dark sorrow rises dim from the edge of the sky.

Grass glows in mist and the last dying light;
in silence, who could read my heart
upon this rail where I stand alone?

I'd cast off all restraint and drink till reason fades,
raise wine, raise song—yet forced mirth
tastes bitter, hollow, without flavor.

My belt loosens, and still I will not rue—
for her I waste to haggard bone and breath,
and I would not trade one thread of this.

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

translation:
By the Xunyang River, I saw a guest off by night,
Amid maple leaves and reed-blossoms in the autumn's cold sigh.
The host dismounted; the guest was already aboard,
We raised our cups to drink, yet no pipes or strings played.
Drunk but joyless, grief loomed at parting—
At parting, the vast river steeped the moon in its flood.
Then, from the water, the sound of a pipa arose;
The host forgot his home, the guest his departure.
We followed the music, whispering, "Who plays?"
The pipa fell silent, then a voice, slow to speak.
We drew our boats close and bade her to come,
Poured more wine, relit the lamps, resumed the feast.
A thousand calls, ten thousand entreaties, before she emerged,
Still cradling the pipa, half-hiding her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked two, three strings—
Before a tune took shape, feeling was already there.
Each string muffled, each note steeped in thought,
As if telling a life of thwarted ambition.
Head bowed, fingers strumming on,
She sang out all the boundless grief within.
Light tremolo, slow twist, sweep and pluck—
First the *Rainbow Skirts*, then the *Six-String* mode.
The thick strings thundered like sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered like lovers' talk.
Thunder and whisper interlaced and played—
Large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then, like orioles warbling beneath blossoms, smooth and bright;
Then, like a spring sobbing beneath ice, slow and choked.
The frozen spring hardened, the strings grew still—
Still and silent, the sound paused for a breath.
Then a hidden sorrow, a dark resentment rose:
In that silence, the sound surpassed all sound.
A silver bottle burst, water spraying forth;
Iron cavalry charged, clashing of blades and spears.
The tune ended; the plectrum swept the center string—
Four strings struck once, like tearing of silk.
East and west boats fell hushed; no one spoke.
Only the autumn moon, white upon the river's heart.
She paused, set the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her dress, rose with a composed face.
She said: "I was a girl of the capital,
My home below Shrimp-Hill, near the old quarter.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name enrolled in the First Troupe of the Academy.
After I played, even the finest masters bowed;
When I made up, courtesans grew jealous.
The young nobles of Five Tombs scrambled to drape me in silk—
One song, and bolts of red gauze, beyond counting they came.
Jeweled pins and silver combs shattered keeping the beat;
Crimson brocade skirts stained by overturned wine.
This year's laughter, next year's laughter again,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent carelessly.
My brother went to the army; my aunt died;
Evening came, morning left, and my beauty faded.
The gate grew cold, horse-and-litter rarely came;
Aging, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes gold, thinks little of parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He leaves; I stay at the river mouth, guard an empty boat;
Around the hull the moon is bright, the river water bitter-cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of girlish days,
Weep in my sleep, and the red tears stain my paint.

I had sighed already at the pipa's voice;
Hearing these words, I sigh again and again.
We are both wanderers cast to the world's far rim—
Since we've met, why should it matter if we knew each other before?

I, since last year, left the Imperial Capital,
Banished, sick in bed, in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, there is no music here;
All year long I hear not the sound of silk and bamboo.
My lodging sits near the Pen River's low damp ground;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo ring my house.
What do I hear each dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding their cry; gibbons moaning in grief.
Spring river, blossom morn, autumn moon night—
I often take wine and pour it for myself alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Their rough, clattering noise is too grating to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's speech,
It is as if I heard fairy music; my ears are clear at last.
Do not refuse—sit down again, play one more song;
For you, I will compose *The Ballad of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stood a long while,
Then sat, drew the strings closer, and the tempo rushed.
Mournful, unlike the earlier sound—
The whole room listened again, and all wept.
Who in that room wept most?
The Blue-Robed Prefect of Jiangzhou: his garment was soaked.

By the Xunyang River, I saw a guest off by night,
Amid maple leaves and reed-blossoms in the autumn's cold sigh.
The host dismounted; the guest was already aboard,
We raised our cups to drink, yet no pipes or strings played.
Drunk but joyless, grief loomed at parting—
At parting, the vast river steeped the moon in its flood.
Then, from the water, the sound of a pipa arose;
The host forgot his home, the guest his departure.
We followed the music, whispering, "Who plays?"
The pipa fell silent, then a voice, slow to speak.
We drew our boats close and bade her to come,
Poured more wine, relit the lamps, resumed the feast.
A thousand calls, ten thousand entreaties, before she emerged,
Still cradling the pipa, half-hiding her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked two, three strings—
Before a tune took shape, feeling was already there.
Each string muffled, each note steeped in thought,
As if telling a life of thwarted ambition.
Head bowed, fingers strumming on,
She sang out all the boundless grief within.
Light tremolo, slow twist, sweep and pluck—
First the *Rainbow Skirts*, then the *Six-String* mode.
The thick strings thundered like sudden rain;
The thin strings whispered like lovers' talk.
Thunder and whisper interlaced and played—
Large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Then, like orioles warbling beneath blossoms, smooth and bright;
Then, like a spring sobbing beneath ice, slow and choked.
The frozen spring hardened, the strings grew still—
Still and silent, the sound paused for a breath.
Then a hidden sorrow, a dark resentment rose:
In that silence, the sound surpassed all sound.
A silver bottle burst, water spraying forth;
Iron cavalry charged, clashing of blades and spears.
The tune ended; the plectrum swept the center string—
Four strings struck once, like tearing of silk.
East and west boats fell hushed; no one spoke.
Only the autumn moon, white upon the river's heart.
She paused, set the plectrum among the strings,
Straightened her dress, rose with a composed face.
She said: "I was a girl of the capital,
My home below Shrimp-Hill, near the old quarter.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa,
My name enrolled in the First Troupe of the Academy.
After I played, even the finest masters bowed;
When I made up, courtesans grew jealous.
The young nobles of Five Tombs scrambled to drape me in silk—
One song, and bolts of red gauze, beyond counting they came.
Jeweled pins and silver combs shattered keeping the beat;
Crimson brocade skirts stained by overturned wine.
This year's laughter, next year's laughter again,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent carelessly.
My brother went to the army; my aunt died;
Evening came, morning left, and my beauty faded.
The gate grew cold, horse-and-litter rarely came;
Aging, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes gold, thinks little of parting—
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He leaves; I stay at the river mouth, guard an empty boat;
Around the hull the moon is bright, the river water bitter-cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dream of girlish days,
Weep in my sleep, and the red tears stain my paint.

I had sighed already at the pipa's voice;
Hearing these words, I sigh again and again.
We are both wanderers cast to the world's far rim—
Since we've met, why should it matter if we knew each other before?

I, since last year, left the Imperial Capital,
Banished, sick in bed, in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, there is no music here;
All year long I hear not the sound of silk and bamboo.
My lodging sits near the Pen River's low damp ground;
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo ring my house.
What do I hear each dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding their cry; gibbons moaning in grief.
Spring river, blossom morn, autumn moon night—
I often take wine and pour it for myself alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Their rough, clattering noise is too grating to bear.
Tonight, hearing your pipa's speech,
It is as if I heard fairy music; my ears are clear at last.
Do not refuse—sit down again, play one more song;
For you, I will compose *The Ballad of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stood a long while,
Then sat, drew the strings closer, and the tempo rushed.
Mournful, unlike the earlier sound—
The whole room listened again, and all wept.
Who in that room wept most?
The Blue-Robed Prefect of Jiangzhou: his garment was soaked.

source.title: 永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古
source.author: 辛弃疾
source.text:
千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？

translation:
Eternal Joy — Remembering the Past at Beigu Pavilion, Jingkou

A thousand ages pass; the rivers and mountains endure,
yet no hero remains where Sun Zhongmou once held his throne.
Dance-halls and song-terraces—
all grace and glory, swept away by rain and gale.
In slanting sun, among wild grass and trees,
in humble lanes and common alleys,
they say Jì Nú once lived.
I recall those years: golden halberds, iron steeds,
a spirit swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger's roar.

The Yuanjia campaign, rash and ill-prepared—
vowing to seal the mound at Langjüxü,
won only a panicked, northward glance.
Forty-three years now; still, in my gaze
I remember the beacon-fires
along the road to Yangzhou.
How can one bear to look back?
Beneath the shrine of Fù Lí,
a riot of sacred crows and festival drums.
Who will ask—
Lian Po, too old now:
can he still eat a full meal?

source.title: 永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古
source.author: 辛弃疾
source.text:
千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？

translation:
Eternal Joy — Remembering the Past at Beigu Pavilion, Jingkou

A thousand ages' rivers, mountains stand—
yet heroes such as Sun Zhongmou, none are found.
Dance terraces and song-stages are gone;
all grace and glamour, weathered by wind and rain.
In slanting sun, among the grass and trees,
in common lanes, they say that Ji Nu dwelt.
I think of those years—golden spears, iron steeds,
a breath swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger.

In Yuanjia's haste they sealed the Langju rite,
yet won but a panicked glance toward the north.
Forty-three years—my gaze still holds the flame
of beacon-fires along the road to Yangzhou.
How can the heart endure the turning back?
Beneath Fotuo's shrine, crows wheel and cry,
the village drums beat out their sacrifice.
Who will come asking, as of Lian Po, old—
"Can he still eat his fill?"

source.author: 王维
source.text:
空山新雨后，天气晚来秋。
明月松间照，清泉石上流。
竹喧归浣女，莲动下渔舟。

source.text:
风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。

万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

translation:
By the Yangtze at Xunyang, I saw a guest off into the night;
maple leaves and reed-blossoms shivered in autumn's chill.
The host dismounted; the guest sat in his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but no pipe or string played.
Drunk yet joyless, the parting weighed heavy with grief;
at the moment of farewell, the vast river drowned the moon.
All at once, over the water, a pipa's voice rose—
the host forgot to go home, the guest held back his sail.
Following the sound, I whispered, "Who is it that plays?"
The pipa fell silent; she lingered, slow to speak.
We drew our boats close together and bade her come forth;
refilled the wine, trimmed the wicks, reopened the feast.
Called a thousand times, she at last emerged,
still cradling the pipa, half-hiding her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked two, three strings—
before the melody formed, feeling already spoke.
Each string muted low, each note laden with thought,
as if telling a lifetime of thwarted ambition.
Eyes cast down, fingers roaming freely,
she played out the boundless sorrows of her heart.
Light gathers, slow twists, sweeps and plucks—
first the *Rainbow Garment*, then the *Six Strings* follow.
The thick strings thunder like sudden rain;
the thin strings whisper like intimate speech.
Thunder and whisper intermingle—
large pearls and small pearls fall upon a jade plate.
Trilling like orioles beneath blossoms, smooth;
choked like a spring struggling beneath ice.
The icy spring, cold and sluggish, the strings freeze, stop;
the frozen silence, unbroken, the sound at rest.
A hidden grief, a secret resentment stirs—
at this moment, silence surpasses all sound.
Then a silver vase bursts, water gushing forth;
iron cavalry charges, blades and spears clash.
The song ends; the pick strikes across the center—
all four strings ring once, like silk tearing apart.
East boats and west barges fell silent, mute;
only the autumn moon, white, floated at the river's heart.
Pausing in thought, she set the pick between the strings,
straightened her clothes, rose with composed dignity.
She said she was a girl of the capital,
home in the shadow of Xiama Hill.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa;
her name ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
When she finished a piece, even the greatest masters bowed;
when fully made up, even the fair Qiuniang grew envious.
Young nobles of the Five Tombs vied to offer silk;
one song earned her bolts of red gauze beyond counting.
Jeweled combs shattered keeping time;
blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.
One year of laughter, then the next;
autumn moons and spring breezes passed as if nothing.
Her brother marched to war, her foster-mother died;
evening and morning wore the color from her face.
The door grew cold, horse and saddle few;
aging, she wed a merchant and took his wife's lot.
The merchant prized profit above parting;
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He came, he went; she guards the empty boat at the river mouth;
moonlight circles the hull, the water cold.
Late at night, she dreams of girlhood;
in the dream she weeps, tears streaking rouge across the railing.
I heard the pipa and sighed;
hearing her words, I sigh again, deeply.
We are both wanderers cast to the world's edge—
meeting here, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
banished, bedridden in Xunyang City.
Xunyang, remote, knows no music;
all year long, no silk-and-bamboo sound reaches my ears.
My home near the Pen River sits low and damp;
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow round the house.
Morning and evening, what do I hear?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons howling grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
I take my wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes?
Their harsh, clashing notes are painful to hear.
Tonight I hear your pipa speak—
as if celestial music cleared my ears at last.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song;
for you, I will compose this *Ballad of the Pipa*.
Moved by my words, she stood a long while;
then sat, tightened the strings, which played more urgently.
Melancholy, unlike the earlier notes;
the whole room, hearing again, covered its face and wept.
Who in the room weeps the most?
The blue robe of the Prefect of Jiangzhou is soaked.

By the Yangtze at Xunyang, I saw a guest off into the night;
maple leaves and reed-blossoms shivered in autumn's chill.
The host dismounted; the guest sat in his boat.
We raised our cups to drink, but no pipe or string played.
Drunk yet joyless, the parting weighed heavy with grief;
at the moment of farewell, the vast river drowned the moon.
All at once, over the water, a pipa's voice rose—
the host forgot to go home, the guest held back his sail.
Following the sound, I whispered, "Who is it that plays?"
The pipa fell silent; she lingered, slow to speak.
We drew our boats close together and bade her come forth;
refilled the wine, trimmed the wicks, reopened the feast.
Called a thousand times, she at last emerged,
still cradling the pipa, half-hiding her face.
She turned the pegs, plucked two, three strings—
before the melody formed, feeling already spoke.
Each string muted low, each note laden with thought,
as if telling a lifetime of thwarted ambition.
Eyes cast down, fingers roaming freely,
she played out the boundless sorrows of her heart.
Light gathers, slow twists, sweeps and plucks—
first the *Rainbow Garment*, then the *Six Strings* follow.
The thick strings thunder like sudden rain;
the thin strings whisper like intimate speech.
Thunder and whisper intermingle—
large pearls and small pearls fall upon a jade plate.
Trilling like orioles beneath blossoms, smooth;
choked like a spring struggling beneath ice.
The icy spring, cold and sluggish, the strings freeze, stop;
the frozen silence, unbroken, the sound at rest.
A hidden grief, a secret resentment stirs—
at this moment, silence surpasses all sound.
Then a silver vase bursts, water gushing forth;
iron cavalry charges, blades and spears clash.
The song ends; the pick strikes across the center—
all four strings ring once, like silk tearing apart.
East boats and west barges fell silent, mute;
only the autumn moon, white, floated at the river's heart.
Pausing in thought, she set the pick between the strings,
straightened her clothes, rose with composed dignity.
She said she was a girl of the capital,
home in the shadow of Xiama Hill.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa;
her name ranked first in the Imperial Music Bureau.
When she finished a piece, even the greatest masters bowed;
when fully made up, even the fair Qiuniang grew envious.
Young nobles of the Five Tombs vied to offer silk;
one song earned her bolts of red gauze beyond counting.
Jeweled combs shattered keeping time;
blood-red silk skirts stained with spilled wine.
One year of laughter, then the next;
autumn moons and spring breezes passed as if nothing.
Her brother marched to war, her foster-mother died;
evening and morning wore the color from her face.
The door grew cold, horse and saddle few;
aging, she wed a merchant and took his wife's lot.
The merchant prized profit above parting;
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He came, he went; she guards the empty boat at the river mouth;
moonlight circles the hull, the water cold.
Late at night, she dreams of girlhood;
in the dream she weeps, tears streaking rouge across the railing.
I heard the pipa and sighed;
hearing her words, I sigh again, deeply.
We are both wanderers cast to the world's edge—
meeting here, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
banished, bedridden in Xunyang City.
Xunyang, remote, knows no music;
all year long, no silk-and-bamboo sound reaches my ears.
My home near the Pen River sits low and damp;
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow round the house.
Morning and evening, what do I hear?
Cuckoos crying blood, gibbons howling grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
I take my wine and pour it alone.
Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes?
Their harsh, clashing notes are painful to hear.
Tonight I hear your pipa speak—
as if celestial music cleared my ears at last.
Do not refuse—sit and play one more song;
for you, I will compose this *Ballad of the Pipa*.
Moved by my words, she stood a long while;
then sat, tightened the strings, which played more urgently.
Melancholy, unlike the earlier notes;
the whole room, hearing again, covered its face and wept.
Who in the room weeps the most?
The blue robe of the Prefect of Jiangzhou is soaked.

source.text:
空山新雨后，天气晚来秋。
明月松间照，清泉石上流。
竹喧归浣女，莲动下渔舟。
随意春芳歇，王孙自可留。

the evening air turns autumn.

clear water glides over stones.

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

translation:
# Song of the Pipa

At Xunyang's river-head I saw a guest off by night,
maple leaves and reed-blossoms shivering in autumn's chill.
I dismounted; my friend was already aboard the boat.
We raised our cups to drink—but no pipes, no strings were here.
Drunk, we found no joy; sorrow hung over parting,
and at the moment of farewell the vast river drowned the moon.
Then, suddenly, from across the water, a pipa's voice arose—
I forgot to go home, my guest forgot to sail.
Following the sound I whispered, "Who is playing?"
The pipa fell silent; a voice about to speak, yet slow.
We drew our boats together, invited her to us,
poured more wine, turned up the lamp, reopened the feast.
Called a thousand times, she emerged at last,
still cradling the pipa, half her face obscured.
She turned the pegs, plucked two or three strings—
before the melody formed, feeling was already there.
Each string veiled, restrained; each note laden with thought,
as if telling of a life's thwarted ambition.
Eyes cast down, her hand trusting the strings, she played on,
saying all the boundless things within her heart.
Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept and plucked—
first the *Rainbow Garments*, then the *Six Strings*.
The thick strings thundered like a sudden rain;
the thin strings whispered like a private talk.
Thundering, whispering, interwoven, played as one—
large pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles' song sliding smooth beneath blossoms;
like a spring's sobbing struggling under ice.
Ice-cold, the strings grew stiff, the sound ceased entirely;
stilled and blocked, the music paused for breath.
Yet another hidden grief, a dark resentment, was born—
and in that silence, no sound surpassed all sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly burst, water flying;
like armored cavalry charging, blades and spears clanging.
The piece ended—she drew the pick across the centre;
four strings struck as one, like silk tearing apart.
East boats, west barges: silent, no one spoke.
Only the autumn moon, white, gleaming on the river's heart.
She paused, set down the pick among the strings,
straightened her sleeves, rose with composed countenance.
She said: "I was a girl of the capital,
my home by the Toad Mound.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
my name stood first in the Music Bureau.
After a piece, even great masters were humbled;
dressed up, I drew the envy of the finest courtesans.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to bind my head with silk;
one song, and bolts of red silk beyond all counting.
Silver combs with jewelled tops shattered keeping time;
blood-red skirts stained by spilt wine.
This year laughter, next year laughter again—
autumn moons and spring winds passed carelessly away.
My brother went off to war; my aunt died;
evenings came and mornings went, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, cold and quiet, few horses came.
Growing old, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes profit, thinks little of parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I guard this empty boat at the river's mouth;
the moon circles the hull, the river water cold.
Deep in the night I dreamed of girlhood suddenly,
and wept in the dream, make-up tears streaking red.
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
hearing these words, I sighed again, deeply.
We are both exiles at the world's far end—
meeting here, what need for prior acquaintance?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
banished, I lie ill in Xunyang's town.
Xunyang is remote; there is no music here—
all year long I hear no silk-and-bamboo sound.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around my house.
Morning and evening, what do I hear?
Cuckoos cry blood; apes wail in grief.
Spring rivers, flower-dawns, autumn-moon nights—
often I take wine and pour, alone.
Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes?
Hoarse and grating, unbearable to the ear.
Tonight I hear your pipa's speech—
like celestial music; my ears are clear once more.
Do not refuse: sit down, play one more piece.
For you, I shall compose this *Song of the Pipa*.
Touched by my words, she stood a long while,
then sat, tightened the strings, and played faster still—
sorrowful, unlike the earlier sound.
The whole room, hearing again, hid their weeping.
Who wept the most in that room?
The Sima of Jiangzhou: his blue robe was wet.
