# Song of the Pipa

At Xunyang's river-head I saw a guest off by night,
maple leaves and reed-blossoms shivering in autumn's chill.
I dismounted; my friend was already aboard the boat.
We raised our cups to drink—but no pipes, no strings were here.
Drunk, we found no joy; sorrow hung over parting,
and at the moment of farewell the vast river drowned the moon.
Then, suddenly, from across the water, a pipa's voice arose—
I forgot to go home, my guest forgot to sail.
Following the sound I whispered, "Who is playing?"
The pipa fell silent; a voice about to speak, yet slow.
We drew our boats together, invited her to us,
poured more wine, turned up the lamp, reopened the feast.
Called a thousand times, she emerged at last,
still cradling the pipa, half her face obscured.
She turned the pegs, plucked two or three strings—
before the melody formed, feeling was already there.
Each string veiled, restrained; each note laden with thought,
as if telling of a life's thwarted ambition.
Eyes cast down, her hand trusting the strings, she played on,
saying all the boundless things within her heart.
Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept and plucked—
first the *Rainbow Garments*, then the *Six Strings*.
The thick strings thundered like a sudden rain;
the thin strings whispered like a private talk.
Thundering, whispering, interwoven, played as one—
large pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles' song sliding smooth beneath blossoms;
like a spring's sobbing struggling under ice.
Ice-cold, the strings grew stiff, the sound ceased entirely;
stilled and blocked, the music paused for breath.
Yet another hidden grief, a dark resentment, was born—
and in that silence, no sound surpassed all sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly burst, water flying;
like armored cavalry charging, blades and spears clanging.
The piece ended—she drew the pick across the centre;
four strings struck as one, like silk tearing apart.
East boats, west barges: silent, no one spoke.
Only the autumn moon, white, gleaming on the river's heart.
She paused, set down the pick among the strings,
straightened her sleeves, rose with composed countenance.
She said: "I was a girl of the capital,
my home by the Toad Mound.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
my name stood first in the Music Bureau.
After a piece, even great masters were humbled;
dressed up, I drew the envy of the finest courtesans.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to bind my head with silk;
one song, and bolts of red silk beyond all counting.
Silver combs with jewelled tops shattered keeping time;
blood-red skirts stained by spilt wine.
This year laughter, next year laughter again—
autumn moons and spring winds passed carelessly away.
My brother went off to war; my aunt died;
evenings came and mornings went, and my beauty faded.
Before my door, cold and quiet, few horses came.
Growing old, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes profit, thinks little of parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I guard this empty boat at the river's mouth;
the moon circles the hull, the river water cold.
Deep in the night I dreamed of girlhood suddenly,
and wept in the dream, make-up tears streaking red.
Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
hearing these words, I sighed again, deeply.
We are both exiles at the world's far end—
meeting here, what need for prior acquaintance?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
banished, I lie ill in Xunyang's town.
Xunyang is remote; there is no music here—
all year long I hear no silk-and-bamboo sound.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow all around my house.
Morning and evening, what do I hear?
Cuckoos cry blood; apes wail in grief.
Spring rivers, flower-dawns, autumn-moon nights—
often I take wine and pour, alone.
Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes?
Hoarse and grating, unbearable to the ear.
Tonight I hear your pipa's speech—
like celestial music; my ears are clear once more.
Do not refuse: sit down, play one more piece.
For you, I shall compose this *Song of the Pipa*.
Touched by my words, she stood a long while,
then sat, tightened the strings, and played faster still—
sorrowful, unlike the earlier sound.
The whole room, hearing again, hid their weeping.
Who wept the most in that room?
The Sima of Jiangzhou: his blue robe was wet.

At Xunyang's river-head I saw a guest off by night,
maple leaves and reed-blossoms shivering in autumn's chill.
I dismounted; my friend was already aboard the boat.
We raised our cups to drink—but no pipes, no strings were here.
Drunk, we found no joy; sorrow hung over parting,
and at the moment of farewell the vast river drowned the moon.
Then, suddenly, from across the water, a pipa's voice arose—
I forgot to go home, my guest forgot to sail.
Following the sound I whispered, "Who is playing?"
The pipa fell silent; a voice about to speak, yet slow.
We drew our boats together, invited her to us,
poured more wine, turned up the lamp, reopened the feast.
Called a thousand times, she emerged at last,
still cradling the pipa, half her face obscured.
She turned the pegs, plucked two or three strings—
before the melody formed, feeling was already there.
Each string veiled, restrained; each note laden with thought,
as if telling of a life's thwarted ambition.
Eyes cast down, her hand trusting the strings, she played on,
saying all the boundless things within her heart.
Lightly gathered, slowly twisted, swept and plucked—
first the *Rainbow Garments*, then the *Six Strings*.
The thick strings thundered like a sudden rain;
the thin strings whispered like a private talk.
Thundering, whispering, interwoven, played as one—
large pearls and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Like orioles' song sliding smooth beneath blossoms;
like a spring's sobbing struggling under ice.
Ice-cold, the strings grew stiff, the sound ceased entirely;
stilled and blocked, the music paused for breath.
Yet another hidden grief, a dark resentment, was born—
and in that silence, no sound surpassed all sound.
Then, like a silver vase suddenly burst, water flying;
like armored cavalry charging, blades and spears clanging.
The piece ended—she drew the pick across the centre;
four strings struck as one, like silk tearing apart.
East boats, west barges: silent, no one spoke.
Only the autumn moon, white, gleaming on the river's heart.
She paused, set down the pick among the strings,
straightened her sleeves, rose with composed countenance.

my home by the Toad Mound.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
my name stood first in the Music Bureau.
After a piece, even great masters were humbled;
dressed up, I drew the envy of the finest courtesans.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to bind my head with silk;
one song, and bolts of red silk beyond all counting.
Silver combs with jewelled tops shattered keeping time;
blood-red skirts stained by spilt wine.

autumn moons and spring winds passed carelessly away.

国破山河在，城春草木深。

白头搔更短，浑欲不胜簪。

translation:
The state lies broken; mountains and rivers remain.
Spring in the city; grass and trees grow deep.
Grieved by the times, flowers splash tears;
Hating parting, birds startle the heart.
Beacon fires have raged three months on end;
A letter from home is worth ten thousand gold.
I scratch my white hair—it grows shorter still,
So thin it can no longer hold a pin.

source.author: 李清照
source.text:
风住尘香花已尽，日晚倦梳头。
物是人非事事休，欲语泪先流。
闻说双溪春尚好，也拟泛轻舟。
只恐双溪舴艋舟，载不动许多愁。

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。

translation:
# The Ballad of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River at night I see a friend depart;
maple leaves and reed blossoms shiver through the autumn's heart.
The host dismounts, the guest climbs aboard his waiting boat;
we raise our cups, but no strings or pipes make music float.
No joy in drunkenness—the parting is bitter, grim;
we gaze at vast waters where the moon sinks dim.
Then, from the river, a pipa's voice rides the span—
the host forgets to go, the guest forgets to sail on.

I trace the sound, ask softly: who plays there?
The pipa falls silent; she hesitates to speak, a prayer.
We draw our boats together, invite her to appear;
more wine is poured, the lamp rekindled, the feast renewed once more.
A thousand calls, ten thousand pleas before she shows her face,
still clutching the pipa, half-hiding her grace.
She turns the pegs, plucks a few strings—before the melody forms,
feeling already wells up, breaking all the norms.

Each string a muffled sigh, each note a weight of thought,
as if she tells of a life in frustration caught.
Eyes lowered, fingers flowing on without a break,
she pours out all the endless things the heart holds deep and aching.
Light sweeps, slow twists, slides and plucks in turn—
first the Rainbow Garb, then the Six Melodious notes to learn.
The thick strings roar like sudden rain in haste;
the thin strings whisper like lovers' hushed embrace.
Roar and whisper, interlaced, they blend—
large pearls and small pearls on a jade platter descend.

Birdsong warbles smooth beneath the bloom;
a spring sobs, choked beneath the ice, in gloom.
The cold spring congeals, the strings grow still;
the flow blocked, the sound retreats, the air goes chill.
Yet a deeper sorrow, hidden resentment, is born—
this silence speaks more loudly than any sound.
Then a silver vase bursts—water jets and sprays!
Iron cavalry charges—blades and spears clash in arrays!
The song ends. She draws the pick across the center string;
four strings crash once—like silk torn in a single rending.
East boats, west barges, all fall still and mute;
only the autumn moon, white on the river's root.

She ponders, lays the pick among the strings,
straightens her dress, composes her face as a queen before kings.
"I was a girl of the capital," she says,
"my home at Frog Hill's foot, in its old days.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa's art;
my name stood first in the Imperial Music's part.
When I played, even the greatest masters bowed in awe;
when dressed, the autumn beauties envied me more.
The young lords of Five Mausoleums vied to gift my head;
one song earned bolts of crimson silk, uncounted, spread.
Jeweled combs snapped keeping time like a beat;
blood-red silk skirts stained by spilled wine's heat.
This year's laughter gave way to next year's same;
autumn moons and spring winds passed without a name.
My brother went to war, my aunt passed on;
dusk to dawn, my beauty faded, gone.
My door grew cold, the horses sparse and few;
I aged and wed a merchant, lost to view.
He prizes profit, cares not for farewell's sting—
last month to Fuliang he went to trade for tea.
Gone and gone again, I guard this empty boat;
the moon circles, the river water cuts like cold.
Deep in the night I dream the girlhood days;
I weep in sleep, my painted tears stain the rails red."

I heard the pipa and sighed;
now hearing her tale, I sigh again, more deeply, wide.
We are both lost wanderers at the edge of the world—
meeting here, what need of past ties unfurled?
Last year I left the imperial capital in shame;
exiled, bedridden, in Xunyang I remain.
Xunyang is remote; no music fills the air—
all year, no strings or flutes reach my ear.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp;
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo ring my camp.
What do I hear from dawn to dusk?
The cuckoo bleeds its cry, the gibbons' mournful tusk.
Spring rivers, flower dawns, autumn moonlit nights—
I pour wine, drink alone beneath the lights.
Are there no mountain songs, no village pipes?
Their cackling, clattering grating barely survives.
Tonight I hear your pipa's tongue—
like celestial music, my ears are briefly young.
Don't refuse—sit again, play one more song;
I'll reweave it as the Pipa Ballad, long.

Moved by my words, she stands long in the night;
then sits, tightens strings, the tempo takes its flight.
The sound is more desolate than before;
the whole room hears again and weeps at the core.
Who weeps most among the gathered crowd?
The blue-robed Sima of Jiangzhou—tears unbound.

source.author: 杜甫
source.text:
风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。

source.text:
我住长江头，君住长江尾。

source.title: 江城子·乙卯正月二十日夜记梦
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。

Ten years apart, life and death, all vast and obscure—
I do not try to think of you, yet cannot forget.
A thousand li, your lone grave; nowhere to speak my desolation.
Even if we met, you would not know me—
dust on my face, frost at my temples.

only tears falling in streams.
I know the place where my heart breaks year after year:
a bright moonlit night, the short pine hill.

只愿君心似我心，定不负相思意。

source.title: 江城子·乙卯正月二十日夜记梦
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。

Leaning long upon the high tower, breeze thin and fine,
My gaze exhausted, spring sorrow rises dark at the sky's rim.
In grass-color, mist, and the afterglow's last gleam—
Silent, who understands my heart upon the rail?

Wine in hand, song on lips—forced joy, yet tasteless all.
My belt grows loose, but never would I rue;
For her, worn to a shadow—I would count no cost.

source.title: 念奴娇·赤壁怀古
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

translation:
The Great River sweeps east,
its waves washing away
the heroes of a thousand ages.
West of the old fortifications,
they say, is the Red Cliff
where Zhou Yu of the Three Kingdoms made his stand.
Jagged rocks pierce the sky,
startling waves beat against the shore,
rolling up a thousand piles of snow.
The land and river are a painting—
how many great men in one age alone!

I think of Gongjin in his prime,
Xiao Qiao newly his bride,
his bearing bold and brilliant.
Feather fan and silk kerchief,
laughing and talking,
the enemy's masts turned to ash and smoke.
My spirit roams that ancient land;
were he to smile at me,
it would be for my too-early grey hair.
This world is but a dream—
I pour a cup of wine
to the river and the moon.

source.title: 江城子·乙卯正月二十日夜记梦
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。

衣带渐宽终不悔，为伊消得人憔悴。

The wind has stilled, dust holds the scent of flowers now all gone;
The sun stands high, too weary to comb my hair.
All things remain, but not the people—everything is done;
I open my mouth to speak, but tears come first.
They say Spring lingers still by Twin Creek's shore,
I've thought to drift there in a light-skinned boat—
but fear this grasshopper hull could never bear
this weight of sorrow, far too heavy for its load.

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。

translation:
The Song of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River, on an autumn night, I saw off a friend; maple leaves and reed flowers rustled cold. The host dismounted, the guest was already aboard; we raised our cups, but no strings played. Drunk yet joyless, grief crept over our parting; when we said farewell, the river was vast, moonlight soaking the water.

Suddenly, over the water, came the sound of a pipa. The host forgot to go home, the guest did not sail. I followed the notes, asked softly who was playing; the pipa stopped, the player hesitated, wished to speak but held her tongue. I moved my boat close, invited her to come out, added wine, trimmed the lamp, and reopened the feast. After a thousand calls and ten thousand entreaties she finally appeared, still half-hiding her face behind the pipa.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings a few times; before a tune had formed, feeling was already there. Each string sighed, each note carried sorrow, as if telling of a lifetime's thwarted ambition. Eyes lowered, she played on casually, pouring out the boundless things in her heart. Light gathers, slow twists, sweeps and flicks—first the *Rainbow Feather*, then the *Six Strings*.

The thick strings thundered like driving rain; the thin strings whispered like private talk. Thunder and whispers intermingled—large pearls, small pearls tumbling into a jade plate. Then, muffled like orioles beneath blossoms, then choked like spring water under ice. The cold spring froze, the strings stilled; stillness, blocked, the sound paused. But a secret grief, a hidden resentment stirred—silence, at that moment, spoke louder than sound.

A silver vase burst, water splashing out; iron cavalry charged, blades clashing. The tune ended—she drew the plectrum across the center strings; four strings snapped like tearing silk. East and west boats lay silent; only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.

She mused, lodged the plectrum in the strings, straightened her clothes, rose, composed her face. "I was a girl of the capital," she said, "living near Shrimp Hill. At thirteen I mastered the pipa, enrolled in the First Division of the Imperial Music Bureau. When I finished a piece, the great masters bowed to me; when I made up my face, even the autumn beauties envied me. Young dukes from the Five Tombs competed to drape red silk on me—for one song I'd receive more bolts than I could count. Gold-inlaid combs shattered keeping time; blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine. Year after year of laughter, autumn moons and spring winds passed idly by. Then my brother joined the army, my auntie died; the evenings came, the mornings went, and my beauty faded. The gate grew cold, the horses dwindled; too old to wait, I married a merchant's wife. My merchant cares only for profit, light about parting—last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea. I stayed behind at the river mouth, guarding an empty boat; moonlight rimmed the hull, the river water was cold. Deep in the night I dreamed of girlhood; I woke weeping, my rouge-streaked tears running down."

I had heard the pipa and sighed already; hearing these words, I sighed again. "We are both lost souls of the world—meeting now, why must we have known each other before?" I left the imperial capital last year, demoted, bedridden in Xunyang. Xunyang is remote, without music; all year round I hear no strings. My dwelling near the Pen River sits low and damp, yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around the house. What do I hear from dawn to dusk? Cuckoos bleeding their cries, gibbons wailing in grief. On spring river's side, in flower mornings or autumn nights, I often take wine and drink alone. Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes? Their crude, harsh tones are unbearable. Tonight I heard your pipa's speech—like celestial music, my ears suddenly clear. Do not refuse—sit down, play once more; I will write for you this Song of the Pipa.

Moved by my words, she stood long, then sat again, drew the strings faster. Desolate, unlike the earlier sound; the whole company, hearing again, covered their faces and wept. Who among them shed the most tears? The blue robe of the Sima of Jiangzhou, soaked through.

source.title: 念奴娇·赤壁怀古
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

## 五项分析结果

### 一、人物与逻辑

| 支持片段 | 分析 |
|---|---|
| "千古风流人物"→"三国周郎赤壁" | 由泛论收束至周瑜，逻辑为"总→分" |
| "遥想公瑾当年" | 以"遥想"标记视角转入追忆，主体为苏轼 |
| "多情应笑我，早生华发" | 周瑜之盛与苏轼之衰形成对比，逻辑为"以人映己" |

**不确定处**：上阕"江山如画，一时多少豪杰"是否仅指周瑜一人，还是兼及其他豪杰（如诸葛亮、曹操），原作未明言，存在歧义。

---

### 二、意象修辞

| 支持片段 | 修辞/意象 |
|---|---|
| "乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪" | 视听通感；"雪"喻浪花（明喻省略） |
| "樯橹灰飞烟灭" | 借代（以船具代战船/曹军）；夸张 |
| "大江东去" | 以水喻时间（通感/隐喻） |
| "羽扇纶巾" | 借代儒将装束，暗示从容 |

**不确定处**："千堆雪"是否兼有"白发"之暗喻（与"早生华发"呼应），原作无明确语义链接，属推测。

---

### 三、情绪推进

| 阶段 | 片段 | 情绪 |
|---|---|---|
| 起 | "大江东去，浪淘尽" | 苍凉、浩叹 |
| 承 | "乱石穿空……千堆雪" | 激昂、壮烈 |
| 转 | "遥想公瑾……灰飞烟灭" | 崇仰、神往 |
| 合 | "多情应笑我……一尊还酹江月" | 自嘲、释然（或悲凉） |

**不确定处**：末句"人间如梦"是超脱还是沉痛，原作语气两可，无外部语境可裁定。

---

### 四、词义典故疑点

| 疑点 | 原文 | 说明 |
|---|---|---|
| "人道是" | "故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁" | "人道是"三字暗示苏轼本人不确定此即真赤壁，存疑语气 |
| "樯橹" | 一作"强虏" | 原作给出"樯橹"，但与部分版本异文不同；此处依所给文本 |
| "小乔初嫁了" | "了"字 | 语气助词，表已然；但周瑜娶小乔在建安四年（199），赤壁之战在建安十三年（208），"初嫁"与战时相隔近十年，时间逻辑存疑 |
| "酹" | "一尊还酹江月" | 以酒浇地祭月，动作本身无典，但"酹"字古义需确认是否仅用于祭神 |

**不确定处**：原作未标注"强虏/樯橹"版本差异，仅凭所给文本无法判断是否为苏轼原笔。

---

### 五、篇章结构

| 部分 | 片段 | 功能 |
|---|---|---|
| 上阕 | "大江东去……一时多少豪杰" | 写景→怀古，由空间（江山）引入时间（豪杰） |
| 下阕 | "遥想公瑾当年……一尊还酹江月" | 写人→感己，由他人（周瑜）回归自身（华发） |

The Great River surges east, its waves washing away a thousand ages of heroes.
West of the old ramparts, they say, lies Red Cliff where Zhou Lang of the Three Kingdoms stood.
Jagged rocks pierce the sky; thundering breakers lash the shore, rolling up a thousand heaps of snow.
The land is a painting — how many heroes filled a single age!

Human life is but a dream; I pour one cup to the river moon.

source.text:
十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。

translation:
Ten years between the living and the dead—both lost in vastness.
Though I try not to think of you, forgetting is impossible.
Your lone grave lies a thousand miles away;
where can I speak this desolation?
Even if we met again, you might not know me—
my face streaked with dust, my temples frosted like snow.

One night a shadowy dream carried me suddenly home.
At the small lattice window, you were combing your hair.
We gazed at one another, wordless,
only tears streaming down in a thousand rows.
I know that year after year, where my heart will break—
under the moonlit night, on the short pine ridge.

Ten years between the living and the dead—both lost in vastness.
Though I try not to think of you, forgetting is impossible.
Your lone grave lies a thousand miles away;
where can I speak this desolation?
Even if we met again, you might not know me—
my face streaked with dust, my temples frosted like snow.

One night a shadowy dream carried me suddenly home.
At the small lattice window, you were combing your hair.
We gazed at one another, wordless,
only tears streaming down in a thousand rows.
I know that year after year, where my heart will break—
under the moonlit night, on the short pine ridge.

translation:
I lean long on the high tower, the breeze a thread so fine—
Gazing far, spring sorrow lifts, dim, from the sky's own edge.
In the last light, grass and mist blur into one;
Silent—what heart could read the thought behind this railing?

I meant to loose my wildness, seek one night of wine,
Raise the cup, let the song rise—yet forced joy tastes of nothing.
My belt grows wide, my frame grows spare, and I shall never regret—
For her, I would wear myself to ruin, and call it worth.

原作：蝶恋花·伫倚危楼风细细，柳永

伫倚危楼风细细，望极春愁，黯黯生天际。
草色烟光残照里，无言谁会凭阑意。
拟把疏狂图一醉，对酒当歌，强乐还无味。
衣带渐宽终不悔，为伊消得人憔悴。

逐句翻译考量：

1. "伫倚危楼风细细" — 独自倚靠在高楼上，微风细细。危楼=高楼。
2. "望极春愁，黯黯生天际" — 极目远望，春愁从天际黯然升起。
3. "草色烟光残照里" — 草色、烟雾般的光影、残阳之中。
4. "无言谁会凭阑意" — 无人能领会我倚栏的心意。
5. "拟把疏狂图一醉" — 打算放纵疏狂，求一醉。
6. "对酒当歌，强乐还无味" — 面对酒、应当歌，勉强欢乐却无味。
7. "衣带渐宽终不悔" — 衣带渐宽（消瘦）终不后悔。
8. "为伊消得人憔悴" — 为了她/他，值得憔悴。

风格上应保持诗意、简洁、有韵律感。柳永此词语言质朴而深情，译文不宜过于华丽，宜取自然流畅的英文诗行。

我来写一个有节奏感、忠于原意的版本：

I lean long on the high tower, the breeze thin and fine,
Gazing far—spring sorrow rises dim from the sky's edge.
In the fading light, grass and mist blur as one,
Silent—who could read the thought behind my railing?

I meant to loose my wildness, seek a single drunken night,
Raise the cup, sing the song—yet forced joy tastes of nothing.
My belt loosens, my frame grows spare, and I shall never regret it:
For her sake, I would waste away to this hollow face.

再打磨一下，让节奏更统一，意象更精确：

"危楼"是高楼/危耸之楼，"high tower"可以。
"风细细"是极细的风，"the breeze, so fine and thin"。
"望极"是极目远望。
"黯黯生天际"是黯然从天际升起。
"草色烟光残照里"——草色、烟光、残照三者交织。
"无言谁会凭阑意"——无人会意。
"拟把疏狂图一醉"——打算以疏狂求一醉。
"对酒当歌"——对酒当歌，曹操典故，此处是面对酒当放歌。
"强乐还无味"——勉强欢乐却无味。
"衣带渐宽终不悔"——衣带渐宽，终不悔。
"为伊消得人憔悴"——为伊消得，人憔悴。"消得"=值得、配得。

最终版：

I linger, leaning on the high tower, the wind a thread so fine;
I gaze to the far edge—spring sorrow rises, dim, from the rim of the sky.
Through grass and haze, in the last light, all blurs as one;
Silent—what soul could know the meaning of this railing?

I meant to cast off restraint, chase a single night of wine,
Raise the cup, lift the song—yet joy forced tastes of nothing at all.
My belt loosens, my body fades, and I shall not regret it:
For her sake, I would wear myself to ruin.

这个版本不错。"For her sake"用"her"是因为柳永词中"伊"多指女性（歌妓/恋人），这是学界主流看法，虽然不确定但作为翻译选择是合理的。

再微调节奏和用词，确保每行有内在韵律：

I lean long on the high tower, the breeze a thread so fine—
Gazing far, spring sorrow lifts, dim, from the sky's own edge.
In the last light, grass and mist blur into one;
Silent—what heart could read the thought behind this railing?

I meant to loose my wildness, seek one night of wine,
Raise the cup, let the song rise—yet forced joy tastes of nothing.

| **情绪推进** | 由惊（疑）→定（望）→沉（思）三级递降；末句"思故乡"为全诗唯一直抒，前六字皆写物 | 推进幅度极小（四句二十字），"思"字力度是否足以收束，抑或依赖读者补白；无时间跨度，情绪近似切片而非弧线 |

translation:
The Great River surges east—
its waves have washed away
the gallant heroes of ages past.
By the old ramparts to the west,
they say, this is Red Cliff
where Zhou of Three Kingdoms stood.

Jagged rocks stab the sky,
stunning breakers pound the shore,
rolling up a thousand heaps of snow.
Land and river, a living scroll—
how many heroes in that age!

I think back to Gongjin then,
when Xiaoqiao had just been wed,
his bearing proud, his spirit keen.
Feather fan and silk-corded cap,
amid laughter and ease,
the warships' masts and oars
turned to ash and vanished in smoke.

My soul roams that ancient land;
my tender heart should mock me—
already hoary with age.
This life is but a dream:
I raise a cup and pour it
to the river and the moon.

source.title: 念奴娇·赤壁怀古
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

translation:
The Great River surges east;
its waves have swept away
the radiant men of a thousand ages.
West of the old fortifications—
they say—lies the Red Cliff
of Zhou, the young hero of the Three Kingdoms.
Jagged rocks pierce the sky,
thundering breakers pound the shore,
churning a thousand heaps of snow.
Land and river, a living scroll—
how many heroes in one passing age!

I recall Gongjin in his prime:
Little Qiao newly wed,
his bearing bold, his spirit aflame.
Feather fan, silk turban—
laughing, chatting,
and masts and oars turned to ash and vanished.
My soul roams the ancient land;
the tender-hearted would surely laugh at me,
turned gray so soon.
This human life is but a dream—
I pour a cup to the moon on the river.

The Great River flows east,
waves washing away all the heroes of a thousand ages.

rolling up a thousand heaps of snow.
Rivers and mountains painted like a scroll—
how many heroes in that single hour!

I recall Gongjin in his prime,
when Little Qiao had just become his bride,
his bearing bold, his spirit radiant.
Feather fan and silk headband,
talking and laughing as masts and oars

churning up a thousand heaps of snow.

Feather fan, silk turban—

My soul roams that ancient land;

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。

translation:
**Ballad of the Pipa**

By the Xunyang River, on a night I saw off a friend—
maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted; my guest waited on the boat.
We raised our cups, but no strings, no pipes sounded.
Drunk yet joyless, we grieved to part;
as we parted, the river spread vast, the moon steeped in its waters.

Then, suddenly, a pipa voice rose from the water—
I forgot to go home; my guest forgot to sail.
I followed the sound, asked softly who was playing;
the pipa stopped, a voice hesitated to speak.
I moved my boat closer, invited her out;
we poured fresh wine, trimmed the lamp, reopened the feast.
Called a thousand times, summoned ten thousand times, at last she came—
still holding her pipa, half-veiling her face.

She turned the pegs, plucked two or three strings;
before the melody formed, feeling already spoke.
Each string a restraint, each note a thought of longing—
as if telling of a life's unfulfilled will.
Head lowered, fingers wandering freely, she played on,
telling all the boundless matters of her heart.
Light pressing, slow twisting, brushing, then lifting—
first the *Rainbow Feather*, then the *Six Strings* followed.

The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
the thin strings whispered like a private murmur.
Rumbling and whispering, intertwined and tossed—
large pearls and small pearls falling on a jade dish.
Sweet and clear as orioles singing beneath blossoms;
muffled and choked as a spring struggling under ice.
Ice-cold, sluggish, the strings froze and ceased—
ceased and blocked, the sound paused for a moment.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment stirred;
this silence surpassed even sound.

Then—silver bottle bursting, water and浆 spraying;
iron cavalry charging, blades and spears clashing.
The piece ended; she swept the pick across the center—
four strings struck once, like silk tearing apart.
East boats and west barges fell utterly silent;
only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.

She pondered, set the pick into the strings,
straightened her clothes, rose, composed her face.
"I was once a girl of the capital," she said,
"my home by the Toad Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
my name stood in the First Division of the Teaching Quarter.
After a piece, even the great masters bowed;
when made up, every beauty envied me.
The young gallants of Five Tombs vied to drape silk on me—
one song, and bolts of red gauze beyond counting.
Gold-inlaid combs, silver hairpins, shattered keeping time;
blood-red skirts stained by spilt wine.
This year of laughter, next year of ease,
autumn moons and spring winds passed idly by.
Then my brother went to war, my auntie died;
evening and morning wore on—my beauty faded.
The gate grew cold, horses and carriages thinned;
past my prime, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes profit, thinks little of parting;
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I kept watch on the empty boat—
the moon wrapped the hull, the river water cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dreamed of girlhood days,
cried in my sleep, and red tears streaked my painted cheeks."

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
hearing these words, I sighed again, and again.
We are both lost souls at the sky's end—
meeting now, why should we have known each other before?

"Since last year I left the imperial capital,
demoted, I lay sick in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
the whole year I hear no strings, no pipes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo growing around my house.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding their cries, gibbons wailing in grief.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
often I take wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Gurgling, grating—impossible to bear.
Tonight I heard your pipa's speech:
like hearing celestial music, my ears suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one piece—
for you I shall compose the *Ballad of the Pipa*."

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
then returned to her seat, tightened the strings, played faster.
Mournful now, unlike the earlier sound—
the whole company, hearing again, covered their faces and wept.
Who among those seated shed the most tears?
The司马 of Jiangzhou—his blue robe soaked through.

|---|---|---|

|---|---|---|

**Ballad of the Pipa**

By the Xunyang River, on a night I saw off a friend—
maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in the autumn chill.
I dismounted; my guest waited on the boat.
We raised our cups, but no strings, no pipes sounded.
Drunk yet joyless, we grieved to part;
as we parted, the river spread vast, the moon steeped in its waters.

Then, suddenly, a pipa voice rose from the water—
I forgot to go home; my guest forgot to sail.
I followed the sound, asked softly who was playing;
the pipa stopped, a voice hesitated to speak.
I moved my boat closer, invited her out;
we poured fresh wine, trimmed the lamp, reopened the feast.
Called a thousand times, summoned ten thousand times, at last she came—
still holding her pipa, half-veiling her face.

She turned the pegs, plucked two or three strings;
before the melody formed, feeling already spoke.
Each string a restraint, each note a thought of longing—
as if telling of a life's unfulfilled will.
Head lowered, fingers wandering freely, she played on,
telling all the boundless matters of her heart.
Light pressing, slow twisting, brushing, then lifting—
first the *Rainbow Feather*, then the *Six Strings* followed.

The thick strings rumbled like a sudden downpour;
the thin strings whispered like a private murmur.
Rumbling and whispering, intertwined and tossed—
large pearls and small pearls falling on a jade dish.
Sweet and clear as orioles singing beneath blossoms;
muffled and choked as a spring struggling under ice.
Ice-cold, sluggish, the strings froze and ceased—
ceased and blocked, the sound paused for a moment.
A hidden sorrow, a secret resentment stirred;
this silence surpassed even sound.

Then—silver bottle bursting, water and浆 spraying;
iron cavalry charging, blades and spears clashing.
The piece ended; she swept the pick across the center—
four strings struck once, like silk tearing apart.
East boats and west barges fell utterly silent;
only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.

She pondered, set the pick into the strings,
straightened her clothes, rose, composed her face.
"I was once a girl of the capital," she said,
"my home by the Toad Hill.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
my name stood in the First Division of the Teaching Quarter.
After a piece, even the great masters bowed;
when made up, every beauty envied me.
The young gallants of Five Tombs vied to drape silk on me—
one song, and bolts of red gauze beyond counting.
Gold-inlaid combs, silver hairpins, shattered keeping time;
blood-red skirts stained by spilt wine.
This year of laughter, next year of ease,
autumn moons and spring winds passed idly by.
Then my brother went to war, my auntie died;
evening and morning wore on—my beauty faded.
The gate grew cold, horses and carriages thinned;
past my prime, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes profit, thinks little of parting;
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, and I kept watch on the empty boat—
the moon wrapped the hull, the river water cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dreamed of girlhood days,
cried in my sleep, and red tears streaked my painted cheeks."

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
hearing these words, I sighed again, and again.
We are both lost souls at the sky's end—
meeting now, why should we have known each other before?

"Since last year I left the imperial capital,
demoted, I lay sick in Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, without music;
the whole year I hear no strings, no pipes.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo growing around my house.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding their cries, gibbons wailing in grief.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
often I take wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Gurgling, grating—impossible to bear.
Tonight I heard your pipa's speech:
like hearing celestial music, my ears suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one piece—
for you I shall compose the *Ballad of the Pipa*."

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
then returned to her seat, tightened the strings, played faster.
Mournful now, unlike the earlier sound—
the whole company, hearing again, covered their faces and wept.
Who among those seated shed the most tears?
The司马 of Jiangzhou—his blue robe soaked through.

What do I hear at dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding their cries, gibbons wailing in grief.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights,
often I take wine and pour it out alone.
Are there no mountain songs and village flutes?
Gurgling, grating—impossible to bear.
Tonight I heard your pipa's speech:
like hearing celestial music, my ears suddenly clear.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one piece—
for you I shall compose the *Ballad of the Pipa*."

Moved by my words, she stood for a long while,
then returned to her seat, tightened the strings, played faster.
Mournful now, unlike the earlier sound—
the whole company, hearing again, covered their faces and wept.
Who among those seated shed the most tears?
The司马 of Jiangzhou—his blue robe soaked through."}

source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

source.author: 辛弃疾
source.text:
千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？

translation:
A thousand ages of rivers and mountains—
where can the hero Sun Zhongmou be found?
Dance halls and song terraces, all their grace
swept away by wind and rain.
In slanting sun, among weeds and trees,
in ordinary lanes, they say Liu Yu once lived.
Recall those years: iron steeds, golden spears,
a breath that swallowed ten thousand li like a tiger.

The Yuanjia emperor, rash and hasty,
longed to seal the mound of Langjuxu—

原作：
空山不见人，但闻人语响。
返景入深林，复照青苔上。

分析中的关键点：
- 人只以声在，视觉缺席、听觉在场
- 空山、深林、青苔构成幽闭冷色；返景（斜阳）为唯一暖光源
- 以声衬寂、以光衬幽
- "返景"= 斜阳返照之光（景=影）
- "柴"通"寨"，地名
- 结构：听觉对→视觉对，感官切换
- 情绪：寂→微动→更深之寂

我需要给出一个高质量的英译。让我考虑几个方案：

方案1（贴近字面）：
Empty mountains, no one to be seen,
Yet the sound of voices drifts.
The returning light enters the deep forest,
Falling once more upon the green moss.

方案2（更诗化）：
In the empty hills, no soul is seen—
only the echo of a voice.
Slanting sun slips into the deep wood
and rests again on the moss.

方案3：
Empty mountain: no one in sight,
yet somewhere a voice rings out.
The last light bends into the deep woods
and touches the green moss once more.

让我再想想，要兼顾：
- "空山不见人" 的"空"和"不见"
- "但闻人语响" 的"但"（only）和"响"（sound/echo）
- "返景入深林" 的"返景"（returning light/sunset slant）和"入"
- "复照青苔上" 的"复"（again）和"照"和"上"

我倾向于一个简洁、有留白感的译法，不要太散文化。

"Empty hills, no person seen—
only voices sounding.
The low sun enters the deep forest
and falls once more on the moss."

或者更紧凑：

"Empty mountain, unseen person—
yet a voice rings.
Returning light enters the deep wood
and rests on the moss again."

让我再打磨，注意节奏和意象的精确：

"Empty hills: no one to be seen,
yet a voice resounds.
The returning light slips into the deep forest
and touches the moss once more."

"resounds" 对应"响"（回响），不错。
"returning light" 对应"返景"。
"slips into" 对应"入"，有动态。
"touches" 对应"照"，轻柔。
"once more" 对应"复"。

但"Empty hills: no one to be seen" 稍显散文化。

另一个尝试：

"Empty mountain, no soul in sight—
only the sound of a voice.
The slant of returning light
falls on the moss again."

"slant" 有斜阳感，"返回的光"。但"slant of returning light" 稍拗口。

再试：

"Empty hills, no one in sight,
yet a human voice rings out.
The sun's return-light enters the deep wood
and rests once more on the moss."

嗯，让我最终定一个版本，平衡忠实与诗意：

"Empty mountain: no person seen,
yet a voice resounds.
Returning light enters the deep forest
and falls once more on the moss."

这个简洁、有留白。"resounds" 有回响感，对应"响"。"Returning light" 对应"返景"。"falls once more" 对应"复照"。"Empty mountain" 对应"空山"。

不过"no person seen" 稍弱。"空山不见人" 是"空山"+"不见人"两部分。"Empty mountain, no one in sight" 更自然。

最终版：

Empty mountain, no one in sight—
yet a voice resounds.
Returning light enters the deep forest
and falls once more on the moss.

我觉得这个好。四行，简洁，留白，对应原作结构。破折号制造停顿，对应"但"字的转折。

等等，"人语响"——是"人语"的"响"，即人说话的声响/回响。"a voice resounds" 可以。或者 "the sound of voices"。"But voices sound" 也短。

让我保持 "yet a voice resounds"——单数voice有"偶闻一语"的意味，与"空山不见人"的孤寂更配。

定稿。

source.text:
千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？

translation:
Eternal rivers and mountains —
nowhere to find a hero, where is Sun Zhongmou?
Dance pavilions, singing terraces:
all their grace swept by rain, scattered by wind.
Slanting sun over grass and trees, common lanes and alleys —
people say Ji Nu once lived here.
Think of those years: golden halberds, iron steeds,
spirit swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger!

The Yuanjia court, rash and hasty,
sought to seal the mound at Wolf Peak —
only to earn a panicked northward glance.
Forty-three years: in my gaze I still remember
the beacon fires along the road to Yangzhou.
How can one bear to look back?
Beneath the shrine of Fuli, crows caw and festival drums beat.
Who asks — like Lian Po grown old —
can he still eat?

source.text:
千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？

逐句翻译考量：

1. "千古江山" — For a thousand ages the rivers and mountains endure
2. "英雄无觅，孙仲谋处" — Nowhere to find a hero like Sun Zhongmou
3. "舞榭歌台" — Dance pavilions, singing terraces
4. "风流总被、雨打风吹去" — All their glory, beaten by rain, swept by wind, gone
5. "斜阳草树，寻常巷陌" — Slanting sun, grass and trees, ordinary lanes and streets
6. "人道寄奴曾住" — They say this is where Ji-nu once lived
7. "想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎" — Recall those years: golden halberds, iron horses, spirit swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger
8. "元嘉草草" — The Yuanjia era rushed

10. "赢得仓皇北顾" — only gained a panicked glance northward
11. "四十三年" — Forty-three years
12. "望中犹记，烽火扬州路" — Looking out, I still remember beacon fires on the Yangzhou road
13. "可堪回首" — How can one bear to look back?

现在整合成有诗感的英文：

For a thousand ages, rivers and mountains remain—
no hero like Sun Zhongmou to be found in this place.
Dance terraces, song-pavilions,
all their grace, by rain beaten, by wind swept away.
Slanting sun, wild grass, trees,
common lanes and streets—
they say Ji-nu once dwelt here.
Think of those years: golden halberds, iron steeds,
a spirit swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger.
The Yuanjia court, in haste, sought the mound at Langjuxu—
and earned only a panicked glance northward.
Forty-three years—
looking out, I still recall
beacon-fires along the Yangzhou road.
How can one bear to turn back?
Beneath Foli's shrine,
a clamor of crows and festival drums.
Who will ask, as of Lian Po grown old:
"Can you still eat a meal?"

A thousand ages pass; the rivers and hills endure—
where is the hero, Sun Zhongmou, to be found?
Dance pavilions, singing terraces—
all their glory, rain-beaten, wind-swept, gone.
Slanting sun, grass, trees,

they say this is where Ji-nu once lived.
Recall those years—golden halberds, iron horses,
a spirit swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger!
The Yuanjia court, reckless, sought Langjuxu's seal,
and won only a panicked glance northward.
Forty-three years—
gazing out, I still remember
beacon-fires along the Yangzhou road.
How can one bear to look back?
Beneath the shrine of Foli,
a burst of crows and festival drums.
Who will ask, as of Lian Po grown old:
"Can you still eat a meal?"

- "where is the hero, Sun Zhongmou, to be found?" 稍显冗长

- "a panicked glance northward" — "仓皇北顾"，回头北望，仓皇失措。"a panicked look northward" 也行。

Forty-three years—
gazing out, I still remember
beacon-fires along the Yangzhou road.
How can one bear to look back?
Beneath the shrine of Foli,

Who will ask, as of Lian Po grown old:
"Can you still eat a meal?"

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。

translation:
The Song of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River, on a night of seeing off a guest,
maple leaves and reed blossoms shiver in autumn's breath.
The host dismounts, the guest is on the boat;
they raise their cups, but no strings are here.
Drunk yet joyless, they grieve at parting—
at parting, the vast river holds the moon submerged.

Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's voice—
the host forgets his way home, the guest delays his sail.
Following the sound, he asks in the dark: who plays?
The pipa stops; the player hesitates to speak.
Boats drawn close, she is invited to appear;
wine is added, lamps turned up, the feast begins anew.
A thousand calls, ten thousand pleads—she finally comes,
still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.

She turns the pegs, plucks two or three strings;
before a tune is formed, feeling is already there.
Each string muffled, each note full of thought,
as if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Brows lowered, fingers move without a plan,
playing out the boundless matters of the heart.
Light gathers, slow twists, sweeps and plucks—
first the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Strings*.

The thick strings boom like a sudden rain;
the thin strings whisper like a private murmur.
Booming and whispering interweave—
large pearls, small pearls, falling on a jade plate.
Smooth as an oriole's song beneath the blossoms,
choked as a spring trapped under ice.
The icy spring, cold and stalled, the strings grow still;
still and blocked, the sound falls silent for a moment.
A hidden sorrow, a secret grief, is born—
at this moment, silence surpasses sound.

A silver vase bursts, water gushes out;
iron cavalry charges, blades and spears clash.
The tune ends; the pick sweeps across the strings;
one stroke, four strings, like silk tearing apart.
East boats, west boats, all fall quiet—
only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.

She pauses, sets the pick between the strings,
straightens her dress, rises with a composed face.
She says: I was a girl of the capital,
my home below the Toad Hill in the city.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa's art,
my name entered the First Section of the Teaching Quarter.
When I finished a piece, even the master players bowed;
when I made my face up, even the beauties envied me.
The young gallants of Five Tombs vied to bind my hair,
one song earned me bolts of red silk beyond counting.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped at the beat,
blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
This year, laughter; next year, laughter still—
autumn moons, spring breezes, spent without care.
Then my brother went to war, my aunt passed on;
evenings came, mornings went, my beauty faded.
The door grew cold, the horses and riders few;
growing old, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes gain, thinks little of parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Gone and gone, I guard my empty boat at the river mouth,
the moonlight circling the hull, the river water cold.
Deep in the night I dreamed of girlhood days;
in the dream I wept, tears staining my rouge.

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
hearing these words, I sigh again and again.
We are both drifters at the edge of the world—
what need to have been acquainted before we met?

I, since last year, left the imperial capital,
demoted, bedridden in the town of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, no music here;
all year long I hear not a single string or flute.
I live near the Pen River, where the ground is low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding their cry, gibbons crying out in grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
often I pour wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes?
They are hoarse and harsh, unbearable to the ear.

Tonight I heard your pipa's words—
as if hearing celestial music, my ears are cleared.
Do not refuse to sit again, play one more piece;
for you I shall remake this *Song of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stood long in thought,
then sat back, drew the strings—the sound grew urgent.
Sorrowful, unlike the voice before—
the full room, hearing again, all hid their faces and wept.
Who among them wept the most?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked.

The Song of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River, on a night of seeing off a guest,
maple leaves and reed blossoms shiver in autumn's breath.
The host dismounts, the guest is on the boat;
they raise their cups, but no strings are here.
Drunk yet joyless, they grieve at parting—
at parting, the vast river holds the moon submerged.

Suddenly, from the water, a pipa's voice—
the host forgets his way home, the guest delays his sail.
Following the sound, he asks in the dark: who plays?
The pipa stops; the player hesitates to speak.
Boats drawn close, she is invited to appear;
wine is added, lamps turned up, the feast begins anew.
A thousand calls, ten thousand pleads—she finally comes,
still holding the pipa, half hiding her face.

She turns the pegs, plucks two or three strings;
before a tune is formed, feeling is already there.
Each string muffled, each note full of thought,
as if telling of a life unfulfilled.
Brows lowered, fingers move without a plan,
playing out the boundless matters of the heart.
Light gathers, slow twists, sweeps and plucks—
first the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Strings*.

The thick strings boom like a sudden rain;
the thin strings whisper like a private murmur.
Booming and whispering interweave—
large pearls, small pearls, falling on a jade plate.
Smooth as an oriole's song beneath the blossoms,
choked as a spring trapped under ice.
The icy spring, cold and stalled, the strings grow still;
still and blocked, the sound falls silent for a moment.
A hidden sorrow, a secret grief, is born—
at this moment, silence surpasses sound.

A silver vase bursts, water gushes out;
iron cavalry charges, blades and spears clash.
The tune ends; the pick sweeps across the strings;
one stroke, four strings, like silk tearing apart.
East boats, west boats, all fall quiet—
only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.

She pauses, sets the pick between the strings,
straightens her dress, rises with a composed face.
She says: I was a girl of the capital,
my home below the Toad Hill in the city.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa's art,
my name entered the First Section of the Teaching Quarter.
When I finished a piece, even the master players bowed;
when I made my face up, even the beauties envied me.
The young gallants of Five Tombs vied to bind my hair,
one song earned me bolts of red silk beyond counting.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped at the beat,
blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
This year, laughter; next year, laughter still—
autumn moons, spring breezes, spent without care.
Then my brother went to war, my aunt passed on;
evenings came, mornings went, my beauty faded.
The door grew cold, the horses and riders few;
growing old, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes gain, thinks little of parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Gone and gone, I guard my empty boat at the river mouth,
the moonlight circling the hull, the river water cold.
Deep in the night I dreamed of girlhood days;
in the dream I wept, tears staining my rouge.

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
hearing these words, I sigh again and again.
We are both drifters at the edge of the world—
what need to have been acquainted before we met?

I, since last year, left the imperial capital,
demoted, bedridden in the town of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, no music here;
all year long I hear not a single string or flute.
I live near the Pen River, where the ground is low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding their cry, gibbons crying out in grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
often I pour wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes?
They are hoarse and harsh, unbearable to the ear.

Tonight I heard your pipa's words—
as if hearing celestial music, my ears are cleared.
Do not refuse to sit again, play one more piece;
for you I shall remake this *Song of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stood long in thought,
then sat back, drew the strings—the sound grew urgent.
Sorrowful, unlike the voice before—
the full room, hearing again, all hid their faces and wept.
Who among them wept the most?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked.

Booming and whispering interweave—
large pearls, small pearls, falling on a jade plate.
Smooth as an oriole's song beneath the blossoms,
choked as a spring trapped under ice.
The icy spring, cold and stalled, the strings grow still;
still and blocked, the sound falls silent for a moment.
A hidden sorrow, a secret grief, is born—
at this moment, silence surpasses sound.

A silver vase bursts, water gushes out;
iron cavalry charges, blades and spears clash.
The tune ends; the pick sweeps across the strings;
one stroke, four strings, like silk tearing apart.
East boats, west boats, all fall quiet—
only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.

She pauses, sets the pick between the strings,
straightens her dress, rises with a composed face.
She says: I was a girl of the capital,
my home below the Toad Hill in the city.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa's art,
my name entered the First Section of the Teaching Quarter.
When I finished a piece, even the master players bowed;
when I made my face up, even the beauties envied me.
The young gallants of Five Tombs vied to bind my hair,
one song earned me bolts of red silk beyond counting.
Gold-inlaid combs snapped at the beat,
blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
This year, laughter; next year, laughter still—
autumn moons, spring breezes, spent without care.
Then my brother went to war, my aunt passed on;
evenings came, mornings went, my beauty faded.
The door grew cold, the horses and riders few;
growing old, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes gain, thinks little of parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
Gone and gone, I guard my empty boat at the river mouth,
the moonlight circling the hull, the river water cold.
Deep in the night I dreamed of girlhood days;
in the dream I wept, tears staining my rouge.

Hearing the pipa, I had already sighed;
hearing these words, I sigh again and again.
We are both drifters at the edge of the world—
what need to have been acquainted before we met?

I, since last year, left the imperial capital,
demoted, bedridden in the town of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, no music here;
all year long I hear not a single string or flute.
I live near the Pen River, where the ground is low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding their cry, gibbons crying out in grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn moonlit nights—
often I pour wine and drink alone.
Are there no mountain songs, no village flutes?
They are hoarse and harsh, unbearable to the ear.

Tonight I heard your pipa's words—
as if hearing celestial music, my ears are cleared.
Do not refuse to sit again, play one more piece;
for you I shall remake this *Song of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stood long in thought,
then sat back, drew the strings—the sound grew urgent.
Sorrowful, unlike the voice before—
the full room, hearing again, all hid their faces and wept.
Who among them wept the most?
The Sima of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked."}

translation:
Through a thousand ages the rivers and mountains remain,
yet no hero is left to seek where Sun Zhongmou once reigned.
Dance-halls and song-stages — all their grace
swept by rain and wind away.
Slanting sun on grass and trees, common lanes and streets:
they say Ji Nu once lived here.
Think of those years — golden halberds, iron steeds,
spirit swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger.
Yuanjia rushed, seeking to seal Wolf Peak,
won only a panicked glance northward.
Forty-three years: in my gaze I still recall
the beacon fires along the Yangzhou road.
How can one bear to look back?
Beneath the Fox Shrine — a clatter of crows and village drums.
Who will ask, as of Lian Po grown old:
can he still eat a full meal?

source.text:
千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

translation:
# The Song of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River, on a night seeing off a guest,
maple leaves and reed blossoms shiver in autumn's breath.
The host dismounts, the guest is already aboard;
we raise our cups but find no strings to play.
Drunk yet joyless, parting brings its grief—
and as we go, the moon lies vast upon the water.

Then, out of nowhere, pipa sounds across the river;
the host forgets to leave, the guest forgets to sail.
We follow the sound, asking softly who plays—
the pipa stops, a voice reluctant to begin.
We draw our boats together, invite her out,
refill the wine, relight the lamps, resume the feast.
After a thousand calls she finally comes,
still holding her pipa, half her face concealed.

She turns the pegs and plucks a few preliminary notes—
before a melody takes shape, feeling is already there.
Each string is pressed, each note is laden thought,
as if telling of a life of thwarted dreams.
Eyes lowered, fingers move with sure, unhurried grace,
pouring out all the boundless things within her heart.
She slides, she bends, she plucks, she strikes again—
first the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Strings* dance.
The thick strings thunder like a sudden downpour;
the thin strings whisper like a private sigh.
Thunder and whisper intermingle—
large pearls, small pearls tumbling into a jade dish.
Then birdsong winding smooth beneath the blossoms,
then a spring choked slow beneath the ice.
The icy spring turns cold, the strings go stiff,
the flow is blocked, the sound falls still.
But in that silence, deeper sorrow stirs—
this quiet speaks more than these voices could.
Then like a silver vase that bursts and spills,
like iron cavalry that charges, swords and lances clashing—
the tune concludes, she draws her pick across,
one stroke, four strings, a sound like tearing silk.
East boat, west boat, all hushed and still;
only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.

She pauses, sets her pick among the strings,
straightens her dress, rises, composes her face,
and says: "I was a girl of the capital,
my home was by the Toad Hill in Chang'an.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa's art,
my name stood first among the teaching quarter's ranks.
When I finished a piece, even the finest masters yielded;
when I dressed, even the fairest courtesans grew jealous.
The young men of the five tombs vied to shower me with gifts—
one song, and bolts of red silk beyond counting.
My jeweled hairpins broke keeping time;
my crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
One year of laughter after another followed—
autumn moons and spring winds passed in idle ease.
Then my brother went to war, my auntie died,
and evening followed morning, and my beauty faded.
My door grew cold, the horses rare;
past my prime, I wed a merchant's wife.
He values profit over parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; I kept this empty boat at the river's mouth,
the moonlight circling, the water cold around me.
Late at night I dream of girlhood days,
and wake weeping, tears smearing rouge upon my face."

I heard the pipa and already sighed;
now hearing these words, I sigh again.
We are both souls adrift beneath the same wide sky—
what need to have been old acquaintances to meet?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
banished, ill, I lie here in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, with no music here;
all year long I hear not one stringed sound.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo circle my home.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk?
The cuckoo's bleeding cry, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On spring river mornings, on autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and pour alone.
Are there not mountain songs and village pipes?
Their crude, discordant noise is barely bearable.
Tonight I hear your pipa's voice—
it is like celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse—sit down and play one more,
and for you I will compose this *Song of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stands a long while,
then sits, tightens the strings—the music turns urgent.
Sorrowful, unlike the earlier sound;
the whole room, hearing again, all press their faces, weeping.
Who among them has shed the most tears?
The blue robe of the Prefect of Jiangzhou is soaked.

refill the wine, relight the lamps, resume the feast.
After a thousand calls she finally comes,
still holding her pipa, half her face concealed.

She turns the pegs and plucks a few preliminary notes—
before a melody takes shape, feeling is already there.
Each string is pressed, each note is laden thought,
as if telling of a life of thwarted dreams.
Eyes lowered, fingers move with sure, unhurried grace,
pouring out all the boundless things within her heart.
She slides, she bends, she plucks, she strikes again—
first the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Strings* dance.
The thick strings thunder like a sudden downpour;
the thin strings whisper like a private sigh.
Thunder and whisper intermingle—
large pearls, small pearls tumbling into a jade dish.
Then birdsong winding smooth beneath the blossoms,
then a spring choked slow beneath the ice.
The icy spring turns cold, the strings go stiff,
the flow is blocked, the sound falls still.
But in that silence, deeper sorrow stirs—
this quiet speaks more than these voices could.
Then like a silver vase that bursts and spills,
like iron cavalry that charges, swords and lances clashing—
the tune concludes, she draws her pick across,
one stroke, four strings, a sound like tearing silk.
East boat, west boat, all hushed and still;
only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.

She pauses, sets her pick among the strings,
straightens her dress, rises, composes her face,
and says: "I was a girl of the capital,
my home was by the Toad Hill in Chang'an.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa's art,
my name stood first among the teaching quarter's ranks.
When I finished a piece, even the finest masters yielded;
when I dressed, even the fairest courtesans grew jealous.
The young men of the five tombs vied to shower me with gifts—
one song, and bolts of red silk beyond counting.
My jeweled hairpins broke keeping time;
my crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
One year of laughter after another followed—
autumn moons and spring winds passed in idle ease.
Then my brother went to war, my auntie died,
and evening followed morning, and my beauty faded.
My door grew cold, the horses rare;
past my prime, I wed a merchant's wife.
He values profit over parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; I kept this empty boat at the river's mouth,
the moonlight circling, the water cold around me.
Late at night I dream of girlhood days,
and wake weeping, tears smearing rouge upon my face."

I heard the pipa and already sighed;
now hearing these words, I sigh again.
We are both souls adrift beneath the same wide sky—
what need to have been old acquaintances to meet?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
banished, ill, I lie here in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, with no music here;
all year long I hear not one stringed sound.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo circle my home.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk?
The cuckoo's bleeding cry, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On spring river mornings, on autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and pour alone.
Are there not mountain songs and village pipes?
Their crude, discordant noise is barely bearable.
Tonight I hear your pipa's voice—
it is like celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse—sit down and play one more,
and for you I will compose this *Song of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stands a long while,
then sits, tightens the strings—the music turns urgent.
Sorrowful, unlike the earlier sound;
the whole room, hearing again, all press their faces, weeping.
Who among them has shed the most tears?
The blue robe of the Prefect of Jiangzhou is soaked."}

# 《琵琶行》五项分析

---

## 一、人物与逻辑

| 支持片段 | 分析 | 不确定处 |
|---|---|---|
| "十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部" | 琵琶女为教坊乐伎，非妓女，身份为宫廷/官方艺人 | "教坊"唐代有内廷与地方之分，此处未明指哪一教坊 |
| "老大嫁作商人妇""商人重利轻别离" | 逻辑链：色衰→嫁商人→商人外出→独守空船 | 商人是否"重利"为白居易主观判断，无直接证据 |
| "同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识" | 全诗逻辑枢纽：以"沦落"统合两条人生轨迹 | 琵琶女自述是否完全属实、有无夸张，诗中无旁证 |
| "我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城" | 白居易自述为江州司马，贬谪身份 | 仅凭本诗无法确认"帝京"具体指长安还是洛阳 |

---

## 二、意象修辞

| 支持片段 | 修辞手法 | 不确定处 |
|---|---|---|
| "大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语" | 比喻（听觉→触觉/场景） | "急雨"与"私语"是否对应琵琶高低音区，无乐理佐证 |
| "大珠小珠落玉盘" | 通感（听觉→视觉/触觉） | "珠"指单音还是连音，有争议 |
| "别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声" | 以"无声"写"有情"，留白修辞 | 此处是否暗合禅宗"不立文字"之意，无文本内证 |
| "银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣" | 比喻（突然爆发），由静转动的节奏 | "银瓶"指汲水瓶还是酒器，诗中无定指 |
| "东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白" | 以景收声，侧面烘托（不写听者反应而写环境） | "秋月白"与开篇"江浸月"形成首尾呼应，是否有意为之无自注 |
| "枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟" | 叠词+环境渲染，奠定萧瑟基调 | "瑟瑟"指风声还是颜色（碧色），两解并存 |

---

## 三、情绪推进

| 阶段 | 支持片段 | 情绪关键词 | 不确定处 |
|---|---|---|---|
| 起·离愁 | "醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月" | 惨淡、茫然 | "惨"为直抒，程度是否夸张无从比较 |
| 转·好奇 | "忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发" | 惊喜、悬念 | 琵琶声为何能"忘归"，仅凭文本为艺术感染力，逻辑上略有跳跃 |
| 承·沉浸 | "四弦一声如裂帛"→"唯见江心秋月白" | 震撼→寂静 | 从极动到极静的转折仅一句之隔，节奏突兀是否为刻意为之 |
| 叙·悲凉 | "去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒" | 孤寂、寒冷 | "梦啼妆泪红阑干"为琵琶女自述，情绪真实度无法验证 |
| 合·共鸣 | "同是天涯沦落人"→"江州司马青衫湿" | 共悲、释放 | "青衫"为八、九品官服色，是否借服饰强化"沦落"身份，属推测 |

---

## 四、词义典故疑点

| 词/典 | 诗中语境 | 常见解释 | 不确定处 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **虾蟆陵** | "家在虾蟆陵下住" | 长安地名，与董氏庄园有关 | 具体位置及是否代指"繁华之地"无本诗内证 |
| **善才** | "曲罢曾教善才服" | 唐代对琵琶名手的尊称 | "善才"是否特指曹善才一系，或泛称高手，无定论 |
| **秋娘** | "妆成每被秋娘妒" | 多为唐代歌女泛称，亦有实指 | 此处为实人还是泛指，诗中未交代 |
| **缠头** | "五陵年少争缠头" | 赠予歌女的锦帛 | "红绡不知数"之"绡"为丝织品，具体价值无从考证 |
| **霓裳/六幺** | "初为霓裳后六幺" | 唐代大曲名 | 演奏顺序是否对应情绪递进（由雅入急），属推测 |
| **浮梁** | "前月浮梁买茶去" | 今江西景德镇一带，唐代茶市 | 商人经营规模、是否长途，诗中无细节 |
| **呕哑嘲哳** | "呕哑嘲哳难为听" | 形容杂乱刺耳之声 | 是否暗含对民间音乐/地方文化的贬抑，有争议 |
| **青衫** | "江州司马青衫湿" | 唐代低品官服色（八、九品着青） | 白居易当时为从九品上，"青衫"与品级吻合，但诗中未明言品级 |

---

## 五、篇章结构

| 段落 | 起止句 | 功能 | 结构特征 | 不确定处 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 序·背景 | "浔阳江头夜送客"→"主人忘归客不发" | 交代时间、地点、事件，引入琵琶声 | 以"无管弦"为因，"琵琶声"为果，设悬念 | 此段是否原为诗序还是正文，版本有异 |
| 一·演奏 | "寻声暗问弹者谁"→"唯见江心秋月白" | 核心：音乐描摹 | 由"邀见"到"演奏"到"曲终"，自成一完整场景；以环境收束 | "千呼万唤始出来"是否夸张琵琶女矜持程度，无旁证 |
| 二·身世 | "沉吟放拨插弦中"→"梦啼妆泪红阑干" | 琵琶女自述，由盛转衰 | 时间线：十三→欢笑→弟走阿姨死→嫁商人→守空船，线性叙事 | 自述为第一人称，白居易是否如实转述，无文本说明 |
| 三·共鸣 | "我闻琵琶已叹息"→"为君翻作琵琶行" | 诗人介入，点明主题 | "同是天涯沦落人"为全诗主旨句，结构上承上（琵琶女）启下（诗人自述） | "翻作"指"按曲调填词"还是"重新创作"，释义有分歧 |
| 四·尾声 | "感我此言良久立"→"江州司马青衫湿" | 再弹一曲，以"泣"收束 | 与开头"醉不成欢"形成闭环；"青衫湿"为全诗情绪终点 | 第二曲"凄凄不似向前声"，是否暗示琵琶女已动真情，属推测 |

**整体结构判断**：叙事（送客）→描写（音乐）→对话（身世）→议论（共鸣）→叙事（再弹），五段式，以"情"贯穿。不确定处：小序（"元和十年……"）是否应计入正文结构，各版本处理不同。

# The Song of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River, on a night seeing off a guest,
maple leaves and reed blossoms shiver in autumn's breath.
The host dismounts, the guest is already aboard;
we raise our cups but find no strings to play.
Drunk yet joyless, parting brings its grief—
and as we go, the moon lies vast upon the water.

Then, out of nowhere, pipa sounds across the river;
the host forgets to leave, the guest forgets to sail.
We follow the sound, asking softly who plays—
the pipa stops, a voice reluctant to begin.
We draw our boats together, invite her out,
refill the wine, relight the lamps, resume the feast.
After a thousand calls she finally comes,
still holding her pipa, half her face concealed.

She turns the pegs and plucks a few preliminary notes—
before a melody takes shape, feeling is already there.
Each string is pressed, each note is laden thought,
as if telling of a life of thwarted dreams.
Eyes lowered, fingers move with sure, unhurried grace,
pouring out all the boundless things within her heart.
She slides, she bends, she plucks, she strikes again—
first the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Strings* dance.
The thick strings thunder like a sudden downpour;
the thin strings whisper like a private sigh.
Thunder and whisper intermingle—
large pearls, small pearls tumbling into a jade dish.
Then birdsong winding smooth beneath the blossoms,
then a spring choked slow beneath the ice.
The icy spring turns cold, the strings go stiff,
the flow is blocked, the sound falls still.
But in that silence, deeper sorrow stirs—
this quiet speaks more than these voices could.
Then like a silver vase that bursts and spills,
like iron cavalry that charges, swords and lances clashing—
the tune concludes, she draws her pick across,
one stroke, four strings, a sound like tearing silk.
East boat, west boat, all hushed and still;
only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.

She pauses, sets her pick among the strings,
straightens her dress, rises, composes her face,
and says: "I was a girl of the capital,
my home was by the Toad Hill in Chang'an.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa's art,
my name stood first among the teaching quarter's ranks.
When I finished a piece, even the finest masters yielded;
when I dressed, even the fairest courtesans grew jealous.
The young men of the five tombs vied to shower me with gifts—
one song, and bolts of red silk beyond counting.
My jeweled hairpins broke keeping time;
my crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
One year of laughter after another followed—
autumn moons and spring winds passed in idle ease.
Then my brother went to war, my auntie died,
and evening followed morning, and my beauty faded.
My door grew cold, the horses rare;
past my prime, I wed a merchant's wife.
He values profit over parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; I kept this empty boat at the river's mouth,
the moonlight circling, the water cold around me.
Late at night I dream of girlhood days,
and wake weeping, tears smearing rouge upon my face."

I heard the pipa and already sighed;
now hearing these words, I sigh again.
We are both souls adrift beneath the same wide sky—
what need to have been old acquaintances to meet?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
banished, ill, I lie here in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, with no music here;
all year long I hear not one stringed sound.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo circle my home.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk?
The cuckoo's bleeding cry, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On spring river mornings, on autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and pour alone.
Are there not mountain songs and village pipes?
Their crude, discordant noise is barely bearable.
Tonight I hear your pipa's voice—
it is like celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse—sit down and play one more,
and for you I will compose this *Song of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stands a long while,
then sits, tightens the strings—the music turns urgent.
Sorrowful, unlike the earlier sound;
the whole room, hearing again, all press their faces, weeping.
Who among them has shed the most tears?
The blue robe of the Prefect of Jiangzhou is soaked.

the pipa stops, a voice reluctant to begin.
We draw our boats together, invite her out,
refill the wine, relight the lamps, resume the feast.
After a thousand calls she finally comes,
still holding her pipa, half her face concealed.

She turns the pegs and plucks a few preliminary notes—
before a melody takes shape, feeling is already there.
Each string is pressed, each note is laden thought,
as if telling of a life of thwarted dreams.
Eyes lowered, fingers move with sure, unhurried grace,
pouring out all the boundless things within her heart.
She slides, she bends, she plucks, she strikes again—
first the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Strings* dance.
The thick strings thunder like a sudden downpour;
the thin strings whisper like a private sigh.
Thunder and whisper intermingle—
large pearls, small pearls tumbling into a jade dish.
Then birdsong winding smooth beneath the blossoms,
then a spring choked slow beneath the ice.
The icy spring turns cold, the strings go stiff,
the flow is blocked, the sound falls still.
But in that silence, deeper sorrow stirs—
this quiet speaks more than these voices could.
Then like a silver vase that bursts and spills,
like iron cavalry that charges, swords and lances clashing—
the tune concludes, she draws her pick across,
one stroke, four strings, a sound like tearing silk.
East boat, west boat, all hushed and still;
only the autumn moon, white on the river's heart.

She pauses, sets her pick among the strings,
straightens her dress, rises, composes her face,
and says: "I was a girl of the capital,
my home was by the Toad Hill in Chang'an.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa's art,
my name stood first among the teaching quarter's ranks.
When I finished a piece, even the finest masters yielded;
when I dressed, even the fairest courtesans grew jealous.
The young men of the five tombs vied to shower me with gifts—
one song, and bolts of red silk beyond counting.
My jeweled hairpins broke keeping time;
my crimson skirts were stained with spilled wine.
One year of laughter after another followed—
autumn moons and spring winds passed in idle ease.
Then my brother went to war, my auntie died,
and evening followed morning, and my beauty faded.
My door grew cold, the horses rare;
past my prime, I wed a merchant's wife.
He values profit over parting—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; I kept this empty boat at the river's mouth,
the moonlight circling, the water cold around me.
Late at night I dream of girlhood days,
and wake weeping, tears smearing rouge upon my face."

I heard the pipa and already sighed;
now hearing these words, I sigh again.
We are both souls adrift beneath the same wide sky—
what need to have been old acquaintances to meet?
Since last year I left the imperial capital,
banished, ill, I lie here in Xunyang town.
Xunyang is remote, with no music here;
all year long I hear not one stringed sound.
I live near the Pen River, low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo circle my home.
What do I hear at dawn and dusk?
The cuckoo's bleeding cry, the gibbon's mournful wail.
On spring river mornings, on autumn moonlit nights,
I often take my wine and pour alone.
Are there not mountain songs and village pipes?
Their crude, discordant noise is barely bearable.
Tonight I hear your pipa's voice—
it is like celestial music; my ears are suddenly clear.
Do not refuse—sit down and play one more,
and for you I will compose this *Song of the Pipa*.

Moved by my words, she stands a long while,
then sits, tightens the strings—the music turns urgent.
Sorrowful, unlike the earlier sound;
the whole room, hearing again, all press their faces, weeping.
Who among them has shed the most tears?
The blue robe of the Prefect of Jiangzhou is soaked."}

The morning rain at Weicheng has settled the light dust,

Morning rain at Weicheng has dampened the light dust,
Inns and willows, green and new, greet the traveler's eye.
Drink one more cup, I urge you, before you must—
West of Yang Pass, no old friend will be by.

The morning rain at Weicheng has settled the light dust,
The inn and the willows, green and fresh, greet the eye.

West of Yang Pass, no old friend will be by.

Morning rain at Weicheng has dampened the light dust,

West of Yang Pass, no old friend will remain.
"there will be no old friend" 也通。

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。
