translation:
On the River Xun at night I see a guest off,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's chill.
I dismount—my guest is already aboard;
We raise our cups, yet no music fills the air.
Tipsy, joyless, we mourn the parting—
The vast river holds the moon in its depths.
Then, sudden from the water, a pipa's cry!
I forget to go home; my guest forgets to sail.

Following the sound, I ask in the dark: who plays?
The strings fall silent, as if she hesitates to speak.
We draw our boats close and invite her forth;
More wine is poured, the lamps turned up, the feast renewed.
Called a thousand times, she finally comes—
Still cradling the pipa, half veiling her face.

She turns the pegs, plucks two or three strings—
Before a tune takes shape, feeling already pours forth.
Each string muffled, each note a sigh,
As if telling of a life of thwarted ambition.
Brows lowered, fingers move at will,
Unraveling all the boundless ache within.
Light press, slow twist, sweep, then pluck—
First the Rainbow Robe, then the Six-String dance.

The thick strings roar like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like secret talk.
Roaring, whispering, tangled together—
Pearls large and small scattering on a jade plate.
Then like orioles singing beneath blossoms, smooth as silk,
Then like a spring choking under ice, slow and hard.
Ice-cold, the strings seize and break;
Seized and broken, sound stills for a breath.
A hidden grief, a buried hate rises—
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
Then a silver bottle bursts—water surges!
Cavalry charges—swords and spears clash!
The tune ends; she strikes the center with her plectrum;
Four strings sound once—like silk tearing.
East boats, west barges: all fall mute.
Only the autumn moon gleams white upon the river's heart.

She pauses, sets the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her dress, composes her face.
She says she was once a girl of the capital,
Her home near Toad Mound in the old days.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa;
Her name was ranked in the First Section of the Academy.
Her playing made the greatest masters bow;
Her beauty drew the envy of every courtesan.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to shower her with silk—
For one song, bolts of red gauze beyond counting.
Her jeweled combs shattered keeping time,
Her blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Laughter year after year,
Spring moons and autumn breezes passed carelessly by.
Then her brother joined the army, her aunt died—
Dawn to dusk, her beauty faded.
Her door grew cold; horse and saddle rare;
Aging, she wed a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes silver, not her company—
Last month to Fuliang he went to buy tea.
Gone, she keeps watch by the river mouth in an empty boat;
Moonlight wraps the hull; the water bites with cold.
Deep at night she dreams of girlhood—
Weeping, her tears stream through rouge across her face.

I heard the pipa and sighed;
Heard her words and sighed again.
We are both souls adrift, cast to the ends of the earth—
Meeting now, what need of knowing before?
Last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished, ill, lodging in Xunyang's walls.
Xunyang is remote; no music here—
All year I hear no strings, no pipes.
Near the Pen River, the ground low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What is heard at dawn, at dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding out their cries; gibbons wailing in grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights—
I often take my cup and pour alone.
Are there hill songs and village flutes? Yes—
But harsh and grating, unbearable to the ear.
Tonight I hear your pipa's speech;
It is music of immortals—my ears are cleansed anew.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I will compose this Song of the Pipa.

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat, tightened the strings, and played—faster now.
Mournful, unlike the sound before;
The whole assembly, hearing again, covered faces and wept.
Who among them shed the most tears?
The Blue-Robed Magistrate of Jiangzhou—his sleeves soaked through.

忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。

千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。

低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。

冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。

银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。

钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。

我来翻译，注意保持意象精确、节奏流畅：

On the River Xun at night I bid farewell to a guest,
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in autumn's breath.
I dismount—my guest is already aboard;
We raise our cups, yet no music fills the air.
Tipsy, joyless, sorrowing at parting—
The vast river holds the moon in its depths.
Then, from the water, the sudden cry of a pipa!
I forget to go home; my guest forgets to sail.

Following the sound, I ask in the dark: who plays?
The strings fall silent, as if she hesitates to speak.
We draw our boats close and invite her forth;
More wine is poured, the lamps are turned up, the feast renewed.
Called a thousand times, she finally comes—
Still cradling the pipa, half veiling her face.

She turns the pegs, plucks two or three strings—
Before a tune takes shape, feeling already pours forth.
Each string muffled, each note a sigh,
As if telling of a life of thwarted ambition.
Brows lowered, fingers move at will,
Unraveling all the boundless ache within.
Light press, slow twist, sweep, then pluck—
First the Rainbow Robe, then the Six Strings dance.

The thick strings roar like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like secret talk.
Roaring, whispering, tangled together—
Pearls large and small scattering on a jade plate.
Then, like orioles singing beneath blossoms, smooth as silk,
Then, like a spring choking under ice, slow and hard.
Ice-cold, the strings seize and break;
Seized and broken, sound stills for a breath.
A hidden grief, a buried hate rises—
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
Then a silver bottle bursts—water surges!
Cavalry charges—swords and spears clash!
The tune ends; she strikes the center with her plectrum;
Four strings sound once—like silk tearing.
East boats, west barges: all fall mute.
Only the autumn moon gleams white upon the river's heart.

She pauses, sets the plectrum in the strings,
Straightens her dress, composes her face.
She says she was once a girl of the capital,
Her home near Toad Mound in the old days.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa;
Her name was ranked in the First Section of the Academy.
Her playing made the greatest masters bow;
Her beauty drew the envy of every courtesan.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to shower her with silk—
For one song, bolts of red gauze beyond counting.
Her jeweled combs shattered keeping time,
Her blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Laughter year after year,
Spring moons and autumn breezes passed carelessly by.
Then her brother joined the army, her aunt died—
Dawn to dusk, her beauty faded.
Her door grew cold; horse and saddle rare;
Aging, she wed a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes silver, not her company—
Last month to Fuliang he went to buy tea.
Gone, she keeps watch by the river mouth in an empty boat;
Moonlight wraps the hull; the water bites with cold.
Deep at night she dreams of girlhood—
Weeping in dreams, her tears stream through rouge across her face.

I heard the pipa and sighed;
Heard her words and sighed again.
We are both souls adrift, cast to the ends of the earth—
Meeting now, what need of knowing before?
Last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished, ill, lodging in Xunyang's walls.
Xunyang is remote; no music here—
All year I hear no strings, no pipes.
Near the Pen River, the ground low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What is heard at dawn, at dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding out their cries; gibbons wailing in grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights—
I often take my cup and pour alone.
Are there hill songs and village flutes? Yes—
But harsh and grating, unbearable to the ear.
Tonight I hear your pipa's speech;
It is music of immortals—my ears are cleansed anew.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I will compose this Song of the Pipa.

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat, tightened the strings, and played—faster now.
Mournful, unlike the sound before;
The whole assembly, hearing again, covered faces and wept.
Who among them shed the most tears?
The Blue-Robed Magistrate of Jiangzhou—his sleeves soaked through.

The vast river holds the moon in its depths.
Then, sudden from the water, a pipa's cry!
I forget to go home; my guest forgets to sail.

Following the sound, I ask in the dark: who plays?
The strings fall silent, as if she hesitates to speak.
We draw our boats close and invite her forth;
More wine is poured, the lamps turned up, the feast renewed.
Called a thousand times, she finally comes—
Still cradling the pipa, half veiling her face.

She turns the pegs, plucks two or three strings—
Before a tune takes shape, feeling already pours forth.
Each string muffled, each note a sigh,
As if telling of a life of thwarted ambition.
Brows lowered, fingers move at will,
Unraveling all the boundless ache within.
Light press, slow twist, sweep, then pluck—
First the Rainbow Robe, then the Six-String dance.

The thick strings roar like sudden rain,
The thin strings whisper like secret talk.
Roaring, whispering, tangled together—
Pearls large and small scattering on a jade plate.
Then like orioles singing beneath blossoms, smooth as silk,
Then like a spring choking under ice, slow and hard.
Ice-cold, the strings seize and break;
Seized and broken, sound stills for a breath.
A hidden grief, a buried hate rises—
At this moment, silence surpasses sound.
Then a silver bottle bursts—water surges!
Cavalry charges—swords and spears clash!
The tune ends; she strikes the center with her plectrum;
Four strings sound once—like silk tearing.
East boats, west barges: all fall mute.
Only the autumn moon gleams white upon the river's heart.

She pauses, sets the plectrum among the strings,
Straightens her dress, composes her face.
She says she was once a girl of the capital,
Her home near Toad Mound in the old days.
At thirteen she mastered the pipa;
Her name was ranked in the First Section of the Academy.
Her playing made the greatest masters bow;
Her beauty drew the envy of every courtesan.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to shower her with silk—
For one song, bolts of red gauze beyond counting.
Her jeweled combs shattered keeping time,
Her blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine.
Laughter year after year,
Spring moons and autumn breezes passed carelessly by.
Then her brother joined the army, her aunt died—
Dawn to dusk, her beauty faded.
Her door grew cold; horse and saddle rare;
Aging, she wed a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes silver, not her company—
Last month to Fuliang he went to buy tea.
Gone, she keeps watch by the river mouth in an empty boat;
Moonlight wraps the hull; the water bites with cold.
Deep at night she dreams of girlhood—
Weeping, her tears stream through rouge across her face.

I heard the pipa and sighed;
Heard her words and sighed again.
We are both souls adrift, cast to the ends of the earth—
Meeting now, what need of knowing before?
Last year I left the imperial capital,
Banished, ill, lodging in Xunyang's walls.
Xunyang is remote; no music here—
All year I hear no strings, no pipes.
Near the Pen River, the ground low and damp,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my home.
What is heard at dawn, at dusk?
Cuckoos bleeding out their cries; gibbons wailing in grief.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights—
I often take my cup and pour alone.
Are there hill songs and village flutes? Yes—
But harsh and grating, unbearable to the ear.
Tonight I hear your pipa's speech;
It is music of immortals—my ears are cleansed anew.
Do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune;
For you, I will compose this Song of the Pipa.

Moved by my words, she stood long in silence,
Then sat, tightened the strings, and played—faster now.
Mournful, unlike the sound before;
The whole assembly, hearing again, covered faces and wept.
Who among them shed the most tears?
The Blue-Robed Magistrate of Jiangzhou—his sleeves soaked through."}

source.author: 杜甫
source.text:
风急天高猿啸哀，渚清沙白鸟飞回。
无边落木萧萧下，不尽长江滚滚来。
万里悲秋常作客，百年多病独登台。
艰难苦恨繁霜鬓，潦倒新停浊酒杯。

source.author: 杜甫
source.text:
国破山河在，城春草木深。
感时花溅泪，恨别鸟惊心。
烽火连三月，家书抵万金。
白头搔更短，浑欲不胜簪。

source.author: 李之仪
source.text:
我住长江头，君住长江尾。
日日思君不见君，共饮长江水。
此水几时休，此恨何时已。
只愿君心似我心，定不负相思意。

source.title: 卜算子·我住长江头
source.author: 李之仪
source.text:
我住长江头，君住长江尾。
日日思君不见君，共饮长江水。
此水几时休，此恨何时已。
只愿君心似我心，定不负相思意。

让我尝试：

I dwell where the Yangtze begins,
You dwell where the Yangtze ends.
Day after day I long for you, yet cannot see you—
We share this same Yangtze water.

When will this water cease to flow?
When will this ache cease to grow?
Only may your heart mirror mine,

让我打磨一下，让它更有韵律感，同时忠实原作。

"我住长江头，君住长江尾"——"头"是源头，"尾"是入海口/末端。

"此水几时休"——这水何时停。
"此恨何时已"——这恨/遗憾何时尽。

"只愿君心似我心"——愿你心像我心。
"定不负相思意"——定不辜负这份相思之意。

Day after day I think of you, yet never see you—

When will this sorrow end?
I only wish your heart were as mine—
then I would never betray this love.

或者用"will surely not betray"来体现"定"的确定性。

then I shall never betray this longing.

嗯，让我定稿。

兴尽晚回舟，误入藕花深处。
争渡，争渡，惊起一滩鸥鹭。

2. 意象修辞：
- 意象：溪亭、日暮、舟、藕花（荷花）、鸥鹭、一滩。
- 修辞：叠句"争渡，争渡"（反复/顶真式重复）；"误入"拟人化？不，是叙述者误入；"惊起"以动写静。

- 常记→沉醉→兴尽→误入→争渡→惊起。从悠然回忆到迷醉到尽兴到意外急迫到惊散。
- 节奏：前两句舒缓，"误入"转折，"争渡"急促，"惊起"爆发后收束。
- 不确定：结尾"惊起一滩鸥鹭"的情绪是懊恼还是惊喜？文本未直接标明。

4. 词义典故疑点：
- "如梦令"：词牌名，此处仅凭文本无法确定典故来源（用户要求不编造资料）。
- "常记"：是"常常记得"还是"曾经记得"（"常"的时间跨度）。
- "沉醉"：是酒醉还是陶醉于景色？文本无"酒"字。

- "一滩鸥鹭"："滩"指水边沙地还是量词（一群）？

- 结构：起（常记溪亭日暮，沉醉不知归路）—承（兴尽晚回舟，误入藕花深处）—转合（争渡，争渡，惊起一滩鸥鹭）。

source.title: 卜算子·我住长江头
source.author: 李之仪
source.text:
我住长江头，君住长江尾。
日日思君不见君，共饮长江水。
此水几时休，此恨何时已。
只愿君心似我心，定不负相思意。

translation:
To the Tune of Bu Suan Zi: I Live at the Yangtze's Head

I live at the Yangtze's head,
you live at the Yangtze's tail.
Day after day I think of you, yet never see you—
we drink the same Yangtze water.

When will this water cease?
When will this sorrow end?
I only wish your heart were like my heart;
then surely we shall not betray this longing.

source.title: 蝶恋花·伫倚危楼风细细
source.author: 柳永
source.text:
伫倚危楼风细细，望极春愁，黯黯生天际。
草色烟光残照里，无言谁会凭阑意。
拟把疏狂图一醉，对酒当歌，强乐还无味。
衣带渐宽终不悔，为伊消得人憔悴。

translation:
I lean upon the rail of the high tower; the breeze is thin and fine.
My gaze reaches the end of the world, where spring sorrow takes its shape,
Gloomily born upon the edge of the distant sky.
Within the fading light, amid the grass and misty haze,
Silent, who understands the meaning of this lonely stand?

I plan to cast off restraint and seek a drunken oblivion,
To sing and drink, yet forced joy leaves a tasteless void.
My belt grows loose, my form wastes away, yet I regret nothing;
For her sake, I willingly endure this lingering decline.

## 《武陵春·春晚》五项分析

**一、人物与逻辑**

- 支持片段：「日晚倦梳头」→「欲语泪先流」→「也拟泛轻舟」→「只恐……载不动」。
- 逻辑链：一个丧夫（或遭乱）南渡后独居的女性，晨起至日中仍无心梳妆→见人欲言而泪先落→听闻春景尚好而生出游之念→最终被"愁"的重量否决。行为从被动（倦、泪）到主动尝试（闻说、拟）再到自我否定（只恐），构成"起念—否决"的微型戏剧。
- 不确定处：「物是人非」是否确指赵明诚之亡，文本未明言；也可能涵盖靖康之变后故土、旧友、藏书的整体丧失。无法仅凭本词锁定单一事件。

**二、意象修辞**

- 支持片段：「风住尘香花已尽」——以"风住"收束动态，"尘香"将落花化为嗅觉残迹，"花已尽"以完成时态封死春天；「舴艋舟，载不动许多愁」——将抽象情感赋予物理重量，以小船（舴艋，极小之舟）作对比容器。
- 修辞：通感（尘→香）、拟物（愁→可载之物）、借小衬大（舴艋之小 vs 愁之多）。
- 不确定处：「尘香」是否兼指"衣香鬓影"之人事余韵，文本无旁证，不宜坐实。

**三、情绪推进**

| 句 | 情绪色 | 幅度 |
|---|---|---|
| 风住尘香花已尽 | 静、灰、收 | 低 |
| 日晚倦梳头 | 倦怠、无念 | 低 |
| 物是人非事事休 | 决绝、全面否定 | 骤升 |
| 欲语泪先流 | 失控、生理化 | 峰值 |
| 闻说双溪春尚好 | 微光、试探 | 回落 |
| 也拟泛轻舟 | 犹疑中的"也许" | 微升 |
| 只恐……载不动许多愁 | 自我否决、重坠 | 终归于无解 |

- 不确定处：「闻说」是他人转述还是自我想象，文本未给出信息源，情绪转折的"外力"程度存疑。

**四、词义典故疑点**

- 「舴艋舟」：本为吴地小艇名（《越绝书》有载），此处取"极小"义作修辞，非专指地理，但李清照南渡后居金华，双溪即金华武义江，用吴越旧称是否有意乡关之叹——文本不足以判定。
- 「武陵春」：词牌名，与陶渊明《桃花源记》之"武陵"是否构成互文（春尽→桃源不可入），仅凭牌名无法坐实，属牌名巧合还是有意选牌，无作者自注可证。
- 「也拟」：「拟」为"打算、想要"，语气极轻，与后「只恐」形成"未成先否"——疑点在于：她是否真的走到溪边？文本止于"恐"，行动未发生，不可读作已出游。

**五、篇章结构**

- 上阕（前四句）：静态、向内、封闭——风止、花尽、日迟、泪落，空间锁死在闺中。
- 下阕（后四句）：动态、向外、开放—再封闭——闻（听）→拟（谋）→恐（退），空间试图打开（双溪、轻舟）又被"载不动"重新压回。
- 结构对称点：上阕以「倦」收，下阕以「恐」收；上阕否定春天（花已尽），下阕否定自救（舟载不动）。两阕各完成一次"否定"，构成平行而非递进。
- 不确定处：词牌本为双调八句，此作未用叠句或换头特殊处理，结构上的"对称"是否有意经营，抑或仅由词牌格律自然形成，无法从文本内证区分。

source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。

translation:
Ten years — the living, the dead, both lost in boundless haze.
I try not to think of you, yet how could I forget?
A lone grave a thousand li away,
nowhere to speak of all this desolation.
Even if we met again, you would not know me —
dust upon my face, my temples white as frost.

Last night, in a dim dream, I suddenly came home:
you at the small latticed window, combing your hair.
We gazed at each other, not a word —
only tears, a thousand rows.
I know where year after year my heart will break:
a bright-moon night, a ridge of short pines.

I lean upon the high tower, the breeze a whisper thin—
gazing far, spring sorrow
rises darkly from the sky's rim.
In grass-hue and mist and the last slant sun,
silent: who reads my heart at the railing?

I resolve to play the wild one, chase a single drunkenness—
wine before me, song upon my lips,
yet forced mirth is tasteless still.
My belt loosens day by day; I shall not rue it—
for thee, I wear myself to ruin.

source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。

相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。

I gaze to the horizon where spring sorrow grows dim.
In the fading light and misty glow of grassy hues,
Silent, no one understands my intent by the rail.

For her sake, I willingly fade into waste.

source.title: 念奴娇·赤壁怀古
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。

source.text:
十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。

translation:
Jiang Cheng Zi: A Dream in the First Month of Yi Mao

Ten years apart, living and dying, all is vast and dim.
Though I do not try to recall, you are unforgettable.
Your solitary grave lies a thousand li away;
I have no place to speak my desolation.
Even if we were to meet face to face, you might not know me—
My face dust-covered, my temples frosted with white hair.

Last night, in a shadowy dream, I suddenly returned home.
By the small window, you were arranging your makeup.
We gazed at each other in silence,
With only tears streaming down in thousand lines.
I imagine that every year, where my heart breaks,
Is under the bright moon’s light, on the hill of short pines.

translation:
Ten years between the living and the dead,
Though I try not to think of you,
I can never forget.
Your lonely grave lies a thousand miles away,
With nowhere to voice my sorrow.
Even if we were to meet again,
You might not know me—
My face dusted with travel,
My temples frosted with age.

Last night in a quiet dream, I suddenly returned home;
At the small window’s pane,
You were just arranging your hair.
We gazed at each other, silent,
Only tears streaming down like rivers.
Year after year, I imagine
Where my heart breaks the most:
Under the bright moon’s glow,
On the short-pine hill.

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

translation:
By the River Xun on a night I saw a guest off,
maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted; the guest was still aboard the boat;
we raised our cups but found no pipes, no strings.
Drunk, no joy; grief pressed us toward farewell—
at parting, vast and dim, the moon sank in the river.

Then, from the water, a pipa's voice!
The host forgot to go; the guest held back his boat.
We traced the sound, asked softly, "Who plays?"
The pipa stopped; the player hesitated, half-awake to speech.
We drew our boats together, bade her come and see;
we topped the wine, relit the lamp, reopened the feast.
Called a thousand times, summoned ten thousand, only then she emerged—
still clasping the pipa, half-hiding her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked two, three strings;
before the tune had formed, the feeling was already there.
Each string a suppressed murmur, each note a brooding thought,
as if telling of a life ill-fated, ambitions thwarted.
Eyes lowered, fingers free, she played on and on,
unearthing every buried thing the heart had kept.
Light gather, slow twist, brush, and flick—
first a *Nishang* melody, then a *Liuyao*.
The bass strings thundered like a sudden downpour;
the treble strings whispered like private talk.
Thunders and whispers tangled and wove—
large pearls and small pearls tumbling onto a jade plate.
Then, the slide of a warbler trilling beneath blossoms;
then, a brook sobbing, choked by ice below.
The cold spring froze, the strings congealed to silence;
congealed, still, the sound held its breath.
And from that stillness, a hidden sorrow, a secret rancour grew—
at that moment, silence surpassed all sound.
Then a silver jar burst, water and pulp spraying;
iron cavalry broke ranks, blades and spears clanging.
The piece ended; she swept the pick across the four strings—
one final slash, like silk tearing.
East boats, west boats: all silent.
Only the autumn moon, white, still in the river's heart.

She paused, withdrew the pick, thrust it between the strings,
straightened her clothes, rose, composed her face.
Then she spoke of herself: "I was a girl of the capital,
my home by the Shrimp Mound in the old ward.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
my name was first on the imperial music academy's roll.
When I finished a piece, even the great masters bowed to me;
when I set my face, even the finest courtesans envied me.
The young lords of Five Tombs fought to drape my head with scarves—
one song, and bolts of red silk went beyond counting.
Gold-inlaid hairpins and silver combs, snapped to time, fell shattered;
blood-red skirts stained by upturned wine.
This year laughter, next year laughter still;
autumn moons, spring breezes—all taken for granted.
Then my brother went off to war; my auntie died;
evenings came, mornings went, and beauty faded.
The door fell silent; horses and carriages thinned.
Getting old, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes profit, weighs farewell as nothing—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; I guard the empty boat at the river mouth,
the moonlight circling the hull, the river-water cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dreamed a girlhood dream,
and woke weeping, tears cutting red lines through my makeup.

I heard the pipa and sighed;
I heard these words and sighed again, heavier still.
We are both fallen souls at the sky's far edge—
meeting here, what does it matter if we never knew each other?

I, too, left the imperial capital last year,
banished, bedridden, in the town of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music—
throughout the year I hear not a thread of silk, not a breath of bamboo.
I live near the Pen River, where the land is low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo ring my dwelling.
What do I hear from dawn to dusk there?
Cuckoos bleeding their cries, gibbons wailing in grief.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn-night moons,
I often take wine and pour it to myself alone.
It's not that there are no mountain songs or village flutes—
but they are croaking, jangling, unbearable to the ear.
Tonight I heard your pipa's tongue;
it was like hearing celestial music—my ears cleared for the first time in months.
Please, do not refuse; sit down again, play one more piece.
For you, I will remake this song: *The Ballad of the Pipa*.

Touched by my words, she stood a long while,
then sat back down, tightened the strings, and played faster.
Sorrowful, nothing like the voice before—
the whole room heard again and covered their faces, weeping.
Who in the room wept the most?
The blue robe of the Prefect of Jiangzhou was soaked.

first a *Nishang* melody, then a *Liuyao*.
The bass strings thundered like a sudden downpour;
the treble strings whispered like private talk.
Thunders and whispers tangled and wove—
large pearls and small pearls tumbling onto a jade plate.
Then, the slide of a warbler trilling beneath blossoms;
then, a brook sobbing, choked by ice below.
The cold spring froze, the strings congealed to silence;
congealed, still, the sound held its breath.
And from that stillness, a hidden sorrow, a secret rancour grew—
at that moment, silence surpassed all sound.
Then a silver jar burst, water and pulp spraying;
iron cavalry broke ranks, blades and spears clanging.
The piece ended; she swept the pick across the four strings—
one final slash, like silk tearing.
East boats, west boats: all silent.
Only the autumn moon, white, still in the river's heart.

She paused, withdrew the pick, thrust it between the strings,
straightened her clothes, rose, composed her face.
Then she spoke of herself: "I was a girl of the capital,
my home by the Shrimp Mound in the old ward.
At thirteen I mastered the pipa;
my name was first on the imperial music academy's roll.
When I finished a piece, even the great masters bowed to me;
when I set my face, even the finest courtesans envied me.
The young lords of Five Tombs fought to drape my head with scarves—
one song, and bolts of red silk went beyond counting.
Gold-inlaid hairpins and silver combs, snapped to time, fell shattered;
blood-red skirts stained by upturned wine.
This year laughter, next year laughter still;
autumn moons, spring breezes—all taken for granted.
Then my brother went off to war; my auntie died;
evenings came, mornings went, and beauty faded.
The door fell silent; horses and carriages thinned.
Getting old, I married a merchant's wife.
The merchant prizes profit, weighs farewell as nothing—
last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left; I guard the empty boat at the river mouth,
the moonlight circling the hull, the river-water cold.
Deep in the night I suddenly dreamed a girlhood dream,
and woke weeping, tears cutting red lines through my makeup.

I heard the pipa and sighed;
I heard these words and sighed again, heavier still.
We are both fallen souls at the sky's far edge—
meeting here, what does it matter if we never knew each other?

I, too, left the imperial capital last year,
banished, bedridden, in the town of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, with no music—
throughout the year I hear not a thread of silk, not a breath of bamboo.
I live near the Pen River, where the land is low and damp,
yellow reeds and bitter bamboo ring my dwelling.
What do I hear from dawn to dusk there?
Cuckoos bleeding their cries, gibbons wailing in grief.
On spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn-night moons,
I often take wine and pour it to myself alone.
It's not that there are no mountain songs or village flutes—
but they are croaking, jangling, unbearable to the ear.
Tonight I heard your pipa's tongue;
it was like hearing celestial music—my ears cleared for the first time in months.
Please, do not refuse; sit down again, play one more piece.
For you, I will remake this song: *The Ballad of the Pipa*.

Touched by my words, she stood a long while,
then sat back down, tightened the strings, and played faster.
Sorrowful, nothing like the voice before—
the whole room heard again and covered their faces, weeping.
Who in the room wept the most?
The blue robe of the Prefect of Jiangzhou was soaked."}

message.content:
By the River Xun on a night I saw a guest off,
maple leaves and reed flowers shivered in the autumn chill.
The host dismounted; the guest was still aboard the boat;
we raised our cups but found no pipes, no strings.
Drunk, no joy; grief pressed us toward farewell—
at parting, vast and dim, the moon sank in the river.

Then, from the water, a pipa's voice!
The host forgot to go; the guest held back his boat.
We traced the sound, asked softly, "Who plays?"
The pipa stopped; the player hesitated, half-awake to speech.
We drew our boats together, bade her come and see;
we topped the wine, relit the lamp, reopened the feast.
Called a thousand times, summoned ten thousand, only then she emerged—
still clasping the pipa, half-hiding her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked two, three strings;
before the tune had formed, the feeling was already there.
Each string a suppressed murmur, each note a brooding thought,
as if telling of a life ill-fated, ambitions thwarted.
Eyes lowered, fingers free, she played on and on,
unearthing every buried thing the heart had kept.
Light gather, slow twist, brush, and flick—
first a *Nishang* melody, then a *Liuyao*.
The bass strings thundered like a sudden downpour;
the treble strings whispered like private talk.
Thunders and whispers tangled and wove—
large pearls and small pearls tumbling onto a jade plate.
Then, the slide of a warbler trilling beneath blossoms;
then, a brook sobbing, choked by ice below.
The cold spring froze, the strings congealed to silence;

source.title: 江城子·乙卯正月二十日夜记梦
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。

translation:
Ten years have passed, and death divides us still;
Though I try not to think, the memory remains.
My wife’s lone grave lies a thousand miles away,
And nowhere can I speak of my desolate soul.
Even if we met, you would not know me now—
My face is dusted by life’s weary road,
And frost has turned my temples’ hair to gray.

Suddenly last night, in dreams, I returned home,
To see you at the small window’s lattice frame,
Arranging hair and applying makeup fine.
We gazed at one another, wordless each,
With only tears cascading down our cheeks, a thousand streams.
I know where my heart breaks year after year:
Beneath the clear moon’s light on that short pine ridge.

伫倚危楼风细细，望极春愁，黯黯生天际。

translation:
The Great River Flows East, Its Waves Washing Away All the Heroes of a Thousand Ages

To the west of the ancient fortress,
People say this is Red Cliff,
Where General Zhou of the Three Kingdoms reigned.

Jagged rocks pierce the sky,
Startling waves crash against the shore,
Rolling up a thousand piles of snow.

The land and river are like a painting,
How many heroes gathered in that time!

Distantly I recall Gongjin in his prime,
When Little Qiao had just married him,
His heroic posture splendid and bright.

With a feather fan and a silk headscarf,
Laughing and chatting, he blew away
The enemy fleet into ash and smoke.

My spirit wanders through the ancient realm;
If my passionate heart could laugh at me,
It would marvel at my prematurely graying hair.

Human life is but a dream—
I offer a cup of wine to the moon on the river.

translation:
Chanting the Long Melody: Reflections on Chibi

The Great River flows east,
Its waves sweeping away all heroes of a thousand ages.
West of the ancient fortifications,
People say this is where Zhou Yu, of the Three Kingdoms, fought at Red Cliff.

Craggy rocks pierce the sky,
Thrilling waves break against the shore,
Rolling up a thousand heaps of snow.
The mountains and rivers are like a painted scroll;
How many great warriors lived in that single moment!

I recall Gongjin in his prime days,
When Little Qiao had just become his bride,
His posture heroic and spirited.
With a feather fan and a silk headscarf,
While chatting and laughing casually, he caused the enemy’s warships to turn to ash and smoke.

Wandering my spirit through the old kingdom,
Sentimental as I am, they would surely laugh at me
For my hair turning gray too soon.
Human life is but a dream;
I offer this cup of wine to the moon over the river.

source.title: 江城子·乙卯正月二十日夜记梦
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。

translation:
**Jiangchengzi: Remembering a Dream on the Night of January 20th, Yi Mao Year**

Ten years of life and death, vast and unknown.
Though I try not to think of you, forgetting is impossible.
Your lonely tomb lies a thousand miles away;
Nowhere can I speak of my desolation.
Even if we were to meet again, you likely would not know me—
My face dusted with the world, my temples frosted with age.

Last night, in a faint dream, I suddenly returned home;
By the small window, you were arranging your hair and adornments.
We gazed at each other, speechless,
Only tears streaming down like a thousand lines.
I reckon that every year, where my heart breaks,
Is beneath the bright moon’s light,
On the short pine hill.

translation:
Ten years have passed, our worlds of life and death vast and unknown;
Though I try not to dwell on it, your memory is etched in stone.
Your lonely grave lies leagues away, a desolate and silent place,
Where I can find no one to tell my grief’s profound embrace.
Even if we met again, you might not know my face—
Dust stains my cheeks, and frost has claimed my hair with grace.

Tonight within a dream, I suddenly returned to home;
At the small window, bright and clear, you sat before me so,
Adjusting your makeup, quiet as the morning light.
We gazed at one another, speechless through the night,
With only tears streaming down, a thousand lines of sorrow deep.

I know that year by year, my heart will break anew,
Beneath the moon’s cold glow, where short pines sway in dew.

source.title: 念奴娇·赤壁怀古
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

translation:
**Niannujiao: Meditations on Red Cliff**

The Great River flows eastward,
Its waves have washed away the heroes of a thousand ages.
On the western side of the old fortress,
People say this is where Zhou Yu of the Three Kingdoms fought at Red Cliff.
Jagged rocks pierce the sky,
Startling waves crash against the shore,
Rolling up heaps of snow.
The land and river are like a painting;
How many heroes emerged in that single moment!

I think back to Gongjin in his prime,
When Little Qiao had just become his bride,
His heroic bearing shining forth.
With a feather fan and silk headscarf,
Amidst laughter and conversation,
The enemy’s fleet turned to ash and smoke.
My spirit wanders through the ancient kingdom;
If my sentimental nature draws a smile, it should be at me,
Who has grown premature gray hair.
Human life is but a dream;
I offer a cup of wine to the river moon.

source.title: 永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古
source.author: 辛弃疾
source.text:
千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？

translation:
Eternal Joy — Remembering the Past at Beigu Pavilion, Jingkou

A thousand ages of rivers and hills;
no hero to be found where Sun Zhongmou once stood.
Dancers' pavilions, singers' terraces —
all their grace swept clean by rain and wind.
Slanting sun on grass and trees,
ordinary lanes and alleys:
they say the boy Jínu once lived here.
Think of those days — golden halberds, iron steeds,
a spirit swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger!

In Yuanjia, rash and hasty,
he meant to seal the mound at Langjü
and won only a panicked glance northward.
Forty-three years —
in my gaze I still recall
the beacons burning along the road to Yangzhou.
How bearable to look back:
beneath the shrine of Fólí,
a chorus of sacred crows and village drums.
Who is left to ask —
Lian Po is old; can he still eat his fill?

source.title: 念奴娇·赤壁怀古
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

translation:
**Niannujiao: Remembering the Past at Red Cliff**

The Great River flows east,
Its waves sweeping away all heroic figures of a thousand ages.
West of the ancient fortress,
People say this is the Red Cliff of Zhou Yu from the Three Kingdoms.
Jagged rocks pierce the sky,
Startling waves crash against the shore,
Rolling up a thousand heaps of snow.
Our rivers and mountains are like a painting;
How many heroes in that brief span of time!

Distantly I recall Gongjin in those years,
When Little Qiao had just become his bride,
His majestic bearing was vibrant and heroic.
With a feather fan and silk headband,
Amidst laughter and conversation,
The enemy’s warships vanished in smoke and ash.
My spirit roams through the ancient land;
Sentimental as I am, they would surely laugh at me,
For my hair has turned white far too early.
Human life is but a dream;
Let me pour a cup of wine to honor the moon on the river.

translation:
**Nian Nu Jiao: Reflections on the Ancient Battlefield of Chibi**

The great river flows east,
Its waves sweeping away
A thousand years of heroic figures.
On the western side of the old fortifications,
People say this is where Zhou Yu of the Three Kingdoms
Made his famous stand at Chibi.
Jagged rocks pierce the sky,
Towering waves crash against the shore,
Rolling up a thousand piles of snow.
The rivers and mountains are like a painting—
How many heroes graced this single moment!

I think back to Gongjin in those days,
When Little Qiao had just married him,
His majestic bearing was spirited and bold.
With a feather fan and a silk headscarf,
He laughed and talked calmly,
Turning the enemy’s warships into ashes and smoke.
My spirit wanders through that ancient land;
Sentimental as I am, they might laugh at me,
For my hair has already turned gray too soon.
Life here is but a dream—
I raise a cup once more to offer libations
To the river moon.

message.content:
**Nian Nu Jiao: Reflections on the Ancient Battlefield of Chibi**

The great river flows east,
Its waves sweeping away
A thousand years of heroic figures.
On the western side of the old fortifications,
People say this is where Zhou Yu of the Three Kingdoms
Made his famous stand at Chibi.
Jagged rocks pierce the sky,
Towering waves crash against the shore,
Rolling up a thousand piles of snow.
The rivers and mountains are like a painting—
How many heroes graced this single moment!

I think back to Gongjin in those days,
When Little Qiao had just married him,
His majestic bearing was spirited and bold.
With a feather fan and a silk headscarf,
He laughed and talked calmly,
Turning the enemy’s warships into ashes and smoke.
My spirit wanders through that ancient land;
Sentimental as I am, they might laugh at me,
For my hair has already turned gray too soon.
Life here is but a dream—
I raise a cup once more to offer libations
To the river moon.

source.title: 永遇乐·京口北固亭怀古
source.author: 辛弃疾
source.text:
千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？

translation:
**Eternal Joy: Memories at Beigu Pavilion in Jingkou**

For ages past, this land and river stand,
Yet no hero like Sun Quan can be found.
The stages of dance and song have vanished;
All elegance swept away by wind and rain.
Through slanting sun and grass-grown trees,
In common lanes and alleys,
They say where Liu Yu once did dwell.
I recall those days—gold spears, iron steeds,
His spirit swallowing ten thousand li, fierce as a tiger.

In Yuanjia, haste led to ruin’s toll,
A futile quest for glory on the frontier,
Only leaving panicked glances northward.
Forty-three years on, my gaze still holds
Memories of beacon fires along Yangzhou.
How painful to look back! Under the shrine of Tuoba Tao,
Crows caw and drums beat for their feast.
Who will ask if Lian Po, now aged,
Can still eat well enough to wield his sword?

translation:
Eternal Joy · Recalling the Past at Beigu Pavilion in Jingkou

For a thousand ages, the mountains and rivers remain,
But where to find a hero like Sun Quan?
Dancing stages and singing towers—
All traces of their romantic grace
Have been swept away by wind and rain.

In slanting sun, among grass and trees,
In common lanes and alleys,
People say that Emperor Wu once lived here.
Imagine those days: golden halberds and iron horses,
His spirit swallowing ten thousand miles, fierce as a tiger.

In Yuanjia’s haste, recklessly he sought glory,
Hoping to seal victory at Langjuxu,
Only to gain hurried retreats and northward glances.
Forty-three years have passed;
Looking back, I still recall the beacon fires along the Yangzhou road.

Can one bear to look again?
Beneath the shrine of Fuli,
Crowds caw and drums beat for folk rites.
Who comes to ask me, this old Lian Po:
Is my strength yet sufficient to eat well?

message.content:
Eternal Joy: Reflecting on the Past at Beigu Pavilion in Jingkou

For a thousand ages, the rivers and mountains remain,
But where to find heroes like Sun Quan, who ruled with might?
The stages for dance and song have faded into air;
Their romantic splendor swept away by wind and rain.

Beneath the slanting sun, among trees and grass,
In common lanes and alleys, they say Liu Yu once lived.
I recall those days of golden spears and iron horses,
When his spirit swallowed ten thousand miles, fierce as a tiger.

In Yuanjia’s haste, attempts were made to seal Mount Langju,
Only to earn a hurried glance back north in defeat.
Forty-three years have passed; looking out, I still remember
The beacon fires along the road to Yangzhou burning bright.

Is it bearable to look back? Beneath Buddha's Shrine,
Crowds gather, drums beat loud, and crows feast on offerings.
Who asks if Lian Po, though old, can still eat enough rice?

translation:
Eternal Joy: Recalling the Past at Beigu Pavilion in Jingkou

For a thousand ages, this land and river endure,
Yet no hero like Sun Quan can be found.
The stages for dance and song have long since vanished,
Their romantic charm washed away by rain and wind.
Beneath the slanting sun, among grassy trees,
In ordinary lanes and alleys, people say
Liu Yu once lived here. I recall those days—
Gilded spears and iron steeds, their spirit
Swallowing ten thousand miles like a tiger’s roar.

Yuanjia era rushed into war without forethought,
To seal the peak of Langju Mountain was sought,
But only panic and glances northward were gained.
Forty-three years later, looking across the expanse,
I still remember the beacon fires along Yangzhou’s road.
How unbearable to look back! Beneath the temple
Of the Northern Wei emperor, crows peck at offerings,
And village drums thunder in mindless festivity.
Who now asks, as with Lian Po in old age,
If he is still strong enough to eat and ride?

source.title: 江城子·乙卯正月二十日夜记梦
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。

Ten years. Life and death—both lost in vast unknowing.
Even unremembered, how could I forget?
A thousand li, her lonely grave—where can I speak my grief?
Even should we meet, she would not know me—
dust on my face, temples white as frost.

In the night, a dim dream, and I was suddenly home.
At the small window, she was arranging her hair.
We gazed at one another, silent,
only tears—a thousand streams.
I know where, year after year, my heart will break:
the moonlit night, the short-pine ridge.

source.text:
千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？

translation:
For a thousand ages the rivers and mountains endure—
where to find a hero? Sun Zhongmou is gone.
Dance-towers, song-platforms—all their grace
swept off by rain and wind.
Slanting sun, grass and trees,
common lanes and alleys—people say Ji-nu once lived here.
Think of that year: golden halberds, iron horses,
a spirit swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger.
Yuanjia in haste,
seeking to seal Langjuxu Mountain,
won only a panicked glance north.
Forty-three years—
still in my gaze I recall
the beacon fires along the Yangzhou road.
How can one bear to look back?
Beneath the Fóli shrine,
a flock of crows and village drums.
Who is there to ask—
Lian Po, grown old,
can he still eat his fill?

让我逐句翻译：

千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
For a thousand ages the rivers and mountains remain; no hero to seek out—where is Sun Zhongmou?

舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
Dance pavilions and song terraces—all their grace swept away by rain and wind.

斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
Slanting sun, grass and trees, common lanes and alleys—people say Ji-nu once lived here.

想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
Think of that year: golden halberds, iron horses, a spirit swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger.

元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
Yuanjia's hasty campaign, seeking to seal Lang Xu Mountain, won only a panicked glance northward.

四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
Forty-three years—still, in my gaze, I recall the beacon fires along the Yangzhou road.

可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
How can one bear to look back? Beneath the Buddha-Wolf shrine, crows and village drums fill the air.

凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？

For a thousand ages, the rivers and hills endure—
where to seek a hero? Sun Zhongmou is gone.
Dance-towers and song-platforms, their grace
swept away by rain and wind.
Slanting sun, grass and trees,
common lanes and alleys—people say Ji-nu once lived here.
Think of that year: golden spears, iron horses,
a spirit swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger.
Yuanjia's hasty march—
to seal Lang Xu Mountain,
won only a panicked backward glance northward.
Forty-three years—
still in my gaze, I recall
the beacon fires along the Yangzhou road.
How can one bear to look back?
Beneath the Wolf-God shrine,
a throng of crows and village drums.
Who is there to ask—
Lian Po, old now,
can he still eat his fill?

"封狼居胥"——狼居胥是山名（今蒙古国境内），"封"是封禅/筑坛祭天。译为"to seal Langjuxu Mountain"。

For a thousand ages the rivers and mountains endure—
where to find a hero? Sun Zhongmou is gone.
Dance-towers, song-platforms—all their grace
swept off by rain and wind.
Slanting sun, grass and trees,
common lanes and alleys—people say Ji-nu once lived here.
Think of that year: golden halberds, iron horses,
a spirit swallowing ten thousand li like a tiger.
Yuanjia in haste,
seeking to seal Langjuxu Mountain,
won only a panicked glance north.
Forty-three years—
still in my gaze I recall
the beacon fires along the Yangzhou road.
How can one bear to look back?
Beneath the Fóli shrine,
a flock of crows and village drums.
Who is there to ask—
Lian Po, grown old,
can he still eat his fill?

这版不错。"Fóli"保留音译更忠实。"eat his fill"比"eat rice"更好，因为原文"饭"是泛指吃饭/饭量，廉颇的典故核心是"一饭斗米"，用"eat his fill"更自然。

source.title: 念奴娇·赤壁怀古
source.author: 苏轼
source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

translation:
The great river rushes east;
its waves have washed away
the shining figures of a thousand years.
West of the old ramparts—
they say this is Red Cliff
where Zhou the Younger of the Three Kingdoms stood.
Jagged rocks pierce the sky,
thundering breakers beat the shore,
churning up a thousand heaps of snow.
Land and river, a painting—
how many heroes in one brief age!

I dream of Gongjin in his prime,
Xiao Qiao newly wed at his side,
his bearing proud, his spirit aglow.
Feathered fan, silk headband—
amid laughter and talk,
the warships crumbled to ash and smoke.
My soul roams that ancient land;
the sentimental must laugh at me
for growing silver hair so soon.
The world is but a dream—
I pour one cup of wine
as libation to the river's moon.

source.text:
十年生死两茫茫，不思量，自难忘。
千里孤坟，无处话凄凉。
纵使相逢应不识，尘满面，鬓如霜。
夜来幽梦忽还乡，小轩窗，正梳妆。
相顾无言，惟有泪千行。
料得年年肠断处，明月夜，短松冈。

translation:
Ten years of life and death, a vast and boundless dark;
Though I do not try to remember,
I cannot forget.
A thousand miles away, your lonely grave;
Nowhere to speak of my desolate sorrow.
Even if we should meet, you would not know me—
My face covered in dust,
My temples white as frost.
In the night, a quiet dream suddenly brought me home;
By the small window,
You were arranging your hair and face.
We looked at each other in silence,
Only a thousand streams of tears.
I know that year after year, my heart will break
On a bright moonlit night,
At the short pine ridge.

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

translation:
The Song of the Pipa  
By Bai Juyi  

On the banks of the Xunyang River, I bid my guest farewell at night;
Maple leaves and reed flowers shiver in the autumn breeze.
I dismount from my horse while he waits in his boat;
We raise our wine cups to drink, yet lack music for the feast.
Drunk but not joyful, we sorrow as parting nears;
At the hour of goodbye, the moon sinks into the vast river’s depths.
Suddenly, over the water, a pipa’s melody is heard:
I forget to return home, and my guest delays his departure.

Following the sound, I softly ask who plays;
The pipa stops, but she hesitates, slow to speak her name.
I move my boat close by, inviting her to show herself;
More wine is poured, lamps are brought back, and the banquet resumes.
After many calls and entreaties, she finally emerges,
Still holding her pipa, half hiding her face behind it.

She turns the pegs and plucks the strings two or three times;
Before the tune takes form, emotion already breathes.
Each note suppressed, each sound laden with thought,
As if telling the story of a life unfulfilled.
With downcast eyes, she plays casually, continuing on,
Expressing all the infinite affairs within her heart.

Lightly gathering, slowly twisting, rubbing then picking—
First she plays the “Rainbow Feather,” then the “Six-String Melody.”
The thick strings rumble like sudden heavy rain;
The thin strings whisper like private murmurs.
Rumbling and whispering, mixed together in play,
Like pearls large and small falling onto a jade plate.

Smooth and flowing, like an oriole singing beneath blossoms;
Choked and sobbing, like a spring struggling under ice.
Ice-cold and stiff, the strings freeze to silence;
Blocked and still, the sound momentarily ceases.

A hidden sorrow and secret resentment arise;
This moment of silence surpasses any sound.
Suddenly, as if a silver vase breaks and water bursts forth,
Or iron cavalry charges out with swords clashing and spears ringing.

When the song ends, she draws the pick across the center of the strings;
One final stroke sounds like tearing silk.
Eastward ships and westward boats fall silent;
All that remains is the white autumn moon reflected in the river’s heart.

She pauses, puts the pick between the strings,
Straightens her clothes, rises, and composes her expression.
She says of herself: "I was born a girl of the capital city,
My home lies below Shama Ling."
"By thirteen, I had mastered the pipa,
My name was listed among the top performers of the Imperial Conservatory."

"After finishing a piece, even great masters would bow to my skill;
Once made up, I would often be envied by beautiful women like Qiuniang."
"Young men of the Five Mausoleums competed to give me gifts;
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk."

"Jeweled hairpins and silver combs were broken tapping to the beat;
Crimson silk skirts stained with spilled wine."
"This year laughter again next year,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by."

"My brother left for military service, my aunt died;
Evenings pass and mornings come, my beauty faded."
"Before my door grew cold and lonely, horses and carriages sparse;
Getting old, I married a merchant’s wife."

"The merchant values profit above all, lightly dismissing separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea."
"He leaves and returns; I guard the empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and the chill of the river waters."

"Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of youthful days;
In dreams I cry, tears staining my makeup, running down my cheeks."

"I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already;
Hearing these words, I sigh further, overcome with grief."
"We are both people lost at the edge of the world;
Since we meet, why must we have known each other before?"

"I too left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie ill in this city of Xunyang."
"Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear no strings nor flutes."

"I live near the Pen River, where the land is low and damp,
Surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo growing around my home."
"What do I hear here at dawn and dusk?
Only cuckoos crying blood and monkeys wailing in grief."

"On spring river flower mornings and autumn moon nights,
Often I take my wine cup alone to drain it myself."
"Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant sounds are hard to listen to."

"Tonight, hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are suddenly cleared."
"Do not refuse to sit further and play another piece;
For you, I shall compose a new ballad, ‘The Song of the Pipa.’"

Moved by my words, she stands for a long time,
Then sits again, tightening the strings which play faster now."
Sorrowful and bleak, unlike the earlier tunes,
Everyone in the room hears again and covers their faces, weeping."

"Who among those seated sheds the most tears?
The Sima of Jiangzhou has soaked his blue robe."

Each note suppressed, each sound laden with thought,

With downcast eyes, she plays casually, continuing on,

My home lies below Shama Ling."

Once made up, I would often be envied by beautiful women like Qiuniang."
"Young men of the Five Mausoleums competed to give me gifts;
For one song, I received countless bolts of red silk."

"Jeweled hairpins and silver combs were broken tapping to the beat;
Crimson silk skirts stained with spilled wine."
"This year laughter again next year,
Autumn moons and spring breezes passed idly by."

"My brother left for military service, my aunt died;
Evenings pass and mornings come, my beauty faded."
"Before my door grew cold and lonely, horses and carriages sparse;
Getting old, I married a merchant’s wife."

"The merchant values profit above all, lightly dismissing separation;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea."
"He leaves and returns; I guard the empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded by bright moonlight and the chill of the river waters."

"Deep in the night, I suddenly dream of youthful days;
In dreams I cry, tears staining my makeup, running down my cheeks."

"I heard the pipa and sighed deeply already;
Hearing these words, I sigh further, overcome with grief."
"We are both people lost at the edge of the world;
Since we meet, why must we have known each other before?"

"I too left the imperial capital last year,
Banished to lie ill in this city of Xunyang."
"Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year long, I hear no strings nor flutes."

"I live near the Pen River, where the land is low and damp,
Surrounded by yellow reeds and bitter bamboo growing around my home."
"What do I hear here at dawn and dusk?
Only cuckoos crying blood and monkeys wailing in grief."

"On spring river flower mornings and autumn moon nights,
Often I take my wine cup alone to drain it myself."
"Are there no mountain songs or village flutes?
Their harsh, discordant sounds are hard to listen to."

"Tonight, hearing your pipa’s language,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears are suddenly cleared."
"Do not refuse to sit further and play another piece;
For you, I shall compose a new ballad, ‘The Song of the Pipa.’"

Moved by my words, she stands for a long time,
Then sits again, tightening the strings which play faster now."
Sorrowful and bleak, unlike the earlier tunes,
Everyone in the room hears again and covers their faces, weeping."

"Who among those seated sheds the most tears?
The Sima of Jiangzhou has soaked his blue robe."

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

translation:
The Ballad of the Pipa

By the Xunyang River, at night I saw off a guest,
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustled in autumn’s chill.
I dismounted from my horse while my guest was still on his boat;
We raised our wine cups, but there were no flutes or strings to play.
Drunk yet not joyful, we grieved at parting;
At the moment of farewell, the vast river bathed the moon.
Suddenly, over the water, came the sound of pipa music;
The host forgot to return home, and the guest delayed his departure.

Following the sound, I asked softly who was playing,
But the pipa music stopped, and the player hesitated to speak.
We moved our boats closer together and invited her to meet us;
More wine was added, lamps turned up, and the feast began anew.
After countless calls and entreaties, she finally appeared,
Still holding her pipa, half-shyly covering her face.

She turned the pegs and plucked the strings two or three times,
Before a melody formed, emotion had already arisen.
Each string mournful, each note full of sorrow,
As if telling of a lifetime unfulfilled ambition.
With downcast eyes, she played with ease, pouring forth,
Singing all the endless affairs of her heart.
Lightly pressing, slowly twisting, sweeping and picking—
First the *Rainbow Skirt*, then the *Six Beats*.

The thick strings thundered like sudden rain,
The thin strings whispered like private talk.
Thunder and whisper mingled in tangled play,
Like large and small pearls falling on a jade plate.
Bottled and flowing, like birdsong sliding beneath flowers,
Choked and sobbing, like spring water struggling under ice.
When cold ice congeals the strings’ flow, silence falls,
And this blocked silence halts the sound briefly.
Then arises a hidden sorrow, a dark resentment—
In that moment, silence surpassed sound.

Suddenly, like a silver vase bursting, water jets forth,
Or iron cavalry charging out, swords and spears clashing.
At the tune’s end, she drew the plectrum across the center strings,
All four chords struck once, tearing silk apart.
East and west boats lay silent, speechless,
Only seeing the white autumn moon at the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum into the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, and composed her face.
She said herself: “Originally a girl from the Capital City,
My home lived near Shrimp-Spider Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s art,
Renowned among the first troupe of the Imperial Conservatory.
After finishing a tune, skilled musicians would admire me;
Once fully made-up, even beauty rivals grew envious.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to give me gifts,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk flowed to me.
Gold-inlaid hairpins and silver combs snapped keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year passing in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent casually.
My brother joined the army, my dear aunt died,
Days and nights passed, fading my youth’s bloom.
Few horses and carriages before my door, neglected,
Aged now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit lightly regarding partings;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days,
I wake crying, tears staining my rouge-streaked face.”

Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply,
And hearing these words, I lamented again profoundly.
We are both wanderers fallen far from home,
Meeting here, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital, demoted,
Lying ill in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year round, I hear no string or bamboo sounds.
Living near the Pen River, low and damp land,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos bleeding their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings with blossoms, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone for myself.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes?
They croak and chatter, hard to bear listening.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears find clarity anew.
Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune,
For you, I will compose this "Ballad of the Pipa."

Moved by my words, she stood still for a long time,
Then sat back down, strumming faster, strings urgent.
Her notes were mournful, unlike those heard before;
Everyone present, hearing them again, wiped away tears.
Who shed most tears in the audience?
The Sima (Prefectural Assistant) of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through.

主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。

弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}

East and west boats lay silent, speechless,
Only seeing the white autumn moon at the river’s heart.

She pondered deeply, inserted the plectrum into the strings,
Straightened her clothes, stood up, and composed her face.
She said herself: “Originally a girl from the Capital City,
My home lived near Shrimp-Spider Hill.
At thirteen, I mastered the pipa’s art,
Renowned among the first troupe of the Imperial Conservatory.
After finishing a tune, skilled musicians would admire me;
Once fully made-up, even beauty rivals grew envious.
Young men of the Five Tombs vied to give me gifts,
For one song, countless bolts of red silk flowed to me.
Gold-inlaid hairpins and silver combs snapped keeping time,
Blood-red skirts stained by spilled wine.
Year after year passing in laughter and joy,
Autumn moons and spring breezes spent casually.
My brother joined the army, my dear aunt died,
Days and nights passed, fading my youth’s bloom.
Few horses and carriages before my door, neglected,
Aged now, I married a merchant as his wife.
Merchants value profit lightly regarding partings;
Last month he went to Fuliang to buy tea.
He left, guarding an empty boat at the river mouth,
Surrounded only by bright moonlight and cold river water.
Late at night, suddenly dreaming of youthful days,
I wake crying, tears staining my rouge-streaked face.”

Hearing the pipa, I sighed deeply,
And hearing these words, I lamented again profoundly.
We are both wanderers fallen far from home,
Meeting here, why must we have known each other before?
Since last year, I left the Imperial Capital, demoted,
Lying ill in the city of Xunyang.
Xunyang is remote, devoid of music;
All year round, I hear no string or bamboo sounds.
Living near the Pen River, low and damp land,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo grow around my house.
What do I hear morning and evening here?
Cuckoos bleeding their cries, monkeys wailing in grief.
On spring river mornings with blossoms, autumn moonlit nights,
Often I take wine and pour it alone for myself.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes?
They croak and chatter, hard to bear listening.
Tonight, hearing your pipa language,
It is like hearing celestial music; my ears find clarity anew.
Please do not refuse to sit again and play one more tune,
For you, I will compose this "Ballad of the Pipa."

Moved by my words, she stood still for a long time,
Then sat back down, strumming faster, strings urgent.
Her notes were mournful, unlike those heard before;
Everyone present, hearing them again, wiped away tears.
Who shed most tears in the audience?
The Sima (Prefectural Assistant) of Jiangzhou, his blue robe soaked through."}

source.text:
大江东去，浪淘尽、千古风流人物。
故垒西边，人道是、三国周郎赤壁。
乱石穿空，惊涛拍岸，卷起千堆雪。
江山如画，一时多少豪杰。
遥想公瑾当年，小乔初嫁了，雄姿英发。
羽扇纶巾，谈笑处、樯橹灰飞烟灭。
故国神游，多情应笑我，早生华发。
人间如梦，一尊还酹江月。

The Great River surges east—
Its waves have swept away all illustrious men of a thousand ages.
West of the old ramparts, they say
This is Red Cliff, where Zhou Lang of the Three Kingdoms held his stand.
Sheer rocks thrust into the sky, thunderous breakers hurl at the shore,
Churning up a thousand drifts of snow.
Land and river, a painted scroll—
How many heroes graced one age alone!

Far I recall Gongjin in his prime,
Xiao Qiao newly wed, his bearing fierce, his spirit ablaze.
Feather fan in hand, silk headband bound,
Amid jest and laughter—masts and oars turned to ash and smoke.
My soul roams that ancient land;
The sentimental, no doubt, would mock me—
Grey hair, come all too soon!
This world is but a dream—
I raise one cup, and pour a libation yet to the moon over the river.

source.author: 辛弃疾
source.text:
千古江山，英雄无觅，孙仲谋处。
舞榭歌台，风流总被、雨打风吹去。
斜阳草树，寻常巷陌，人道寄奴曾住。
想当年，金戈铁马，气吞万里如虎。
元嘉草草，封狼居胥，赢得仓皇北顾。
四十三年，望中犹记，烽火扬州路。
可堪回首，佛狸祠下，一片神鸦社鼓。
凭谁问、廉颇老矣，尚能饭否？

translation:
Eternal the rivers, eternal the hills—
no hero to find where Sun Zhongmou once stood.
Dance pavilions, singing terraces,
all that grace and flair,
swept away by rain and wind.
Slanting sun, weeds, and trees;
common lanes, humble streets—
"Here," they say, "Jinu once lived."
Think of those days: golden halberds, iron steeds,
a breath that swallowed ten thousand li, fierce as a tiger!

In Yuanjia, rashly they set out
to seal the peak at Wolf Mountain—
all they won was a panicked glance northward.
Forty-three years: in my sight I still recall
the beacon fires along the road to Yangzhou.
How can one bear to look back—
beneath the shrine of Foxi,
crows wheel above the drumming of the harvest feast.
Who comes to ask
whether old Lian Po,
though white-haired, can still eat well enough?

感时花溅泪，恨别鸟惊心。
烽火连三月，家书抵万金。
白头搔更短，浑欲不胜簪。

source.title: 琵琶行
source.author: 白居易
source.text:
浔阳江头夜送客，枫叶荻花秋瑟瑟。
主人下马客在船，举酒欲饮无管弦。
醉不成欢惨将别，别时茫茫江浸月。
忽闻水上琵琶声，主人忘归客不发。
寻声暗问弹者谁，琵琶声停欲语迟。
移船相近邀相见，添酒回灯重开宴。
千呼万唤始出来，犹抱琵琶半遮面。
转轴拨弦三两声，未成曲调先有情。
弦弦掩抑声声思，似诉平生不得志。
低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。
大弦嘈嘈如急雨，小弦切切如私语。
嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。

translation:
**Song of the Pipa**

By night I bid farewell to my guest by the banks of Xunyang;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
I dismount, he steps aboard his boat, we raise our wine-cups high,
But no music plays to fill the air or lift our spirits sky.
Though drunk, joy remains elusive; sorrow looms before parting;
At separation’s hour, the moon sinks deep into the river’s mirroring.

Suddenly, from across the water, the pipa’s notes arise;
Host forgets to go home, guest delays to set out under skies.
Seeking the source, I ask softly who is playing so sweetly;
The pipa pauses, hesitant, as if words are locked tightly.
We move our boats close together, inviting her to appear;
More wine is poured, lamps re-lit, the banquet starts anew here.
After calling ten thousand times, she finally emerges shy,
Still holding her pipa close, half hiding face from eye.

She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, a few preliminary sounds;
Before the melody forms, emotion already abounds.
Each string suppresses sighs, each note conveys deep longing,
As if telling of a lifetime spent in unfulfilled yearning.
Eyes lowered, fingers move freely, strumming continuous lines,
Expressing all the infinite sorrows within her mind.
Light gathering, slow twisting, sweeping then picking once more,
First "Rainbow Garments" dances, then "Six Strings" on the floor.

The thick strings thunder loudly, like rain pouring down fast;
The thin strings whisper softly, voices hushed at last.
Loud and soft intertwined, they play in complex harmony,
Like pearls large and small falling onto a jade tray, vividly.
Melodious as orioles singing beneath bright flower blooms,
Choked and sobbing like spring waters trapped under ice’s glooms.
When the icy stream chokes cold, strings seem frozen and still,
Blocked and silent for a moment, breath held tight against will.

Hidden grief and secret resentments now begin to stir;
In this silence, sound speaks louder than any word ever were.
Then silver vases shatter suddenly, water bursts forth strong,
Iron cavalry charge forward, swords and spears clash along.
The song ends; she draws the plectrum across the center strings,
Four chords ring out sharply, tearing silk with violent springs.
Boats east and west fall silent, no one dares speak a word,
Only seeing the autumn moon shine white where river curved.

She hesitates, inserts the pick between the strings’ tension,
Straightens clothes, composes face, showing dignified repentance.
“I was born,” she says, “a girl of the imperial capital’s heart,
Living near the Toad Mound Hill, since childhood’s early start.
At thirteen, I mastered pipa art, fame reached far and wide,
Ranked first among the Imperial Music Academy’s pride.
After performances, even masters bowed to my skill’s grace,
My beauty made rival courtesans jealous in their place.
Young nobles from Five Tombs fought to offer me their gifts,
Red silk scarves piled high, counting countless shifts.
Gold-inlaid hairpins snapped when keeping time with beats,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine, memories bittersweet.
Year after year of laughter passed, seasons flew away,
Autumn moons, spring breezes wasted carelessly by day.

Brother joined the army; auntie died; youth faded fast,
Dusk gave way to dawn, beauty vanished, shadows cast.
Front door grew desolate, horses rare, visitors few,
Old and weary, I married a merchant, bound to him too.
He values profit over love, cares little for goodbye,
Last month went to Fuliang town to buy tea, leaving dry.
Since he left, I guard an empty boat at river mouth alone,
Surrounded by clear moonlight, cold water flowing tone.
Deep in night, dreams return to days of girlish delight,
Waking tears stain rouge cheeks, running red through the night.”

Hearing the pipa, I had sighed deeply already sore,
Now these words add weight upon my chest, making grief more.
Both of us are exiled souls wandering ends of earth,
Meeting now, why need we know what happened before birth?

Since last year I left the capital, demoted and ill,
Stuck in Xunyang City, resting poor, quiet and still.
This remote place knows no music, silk sounds never reach,
All year long, ears starve for melodies beyond speech.
Living near Pen River, ground low and damp with mist,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround where I exist.
Morning and evening, what do I hear but cries of pain?
Cuckoos bleeding red voices, monkeys wailing in vain.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights beneath moon’s glow,
Often take up wine alone, letting sorrow flow.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes to cheer?
Crude and noisy sounds hard to bear, bringing fear.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech, celestial tones rise clear,
Like listening to immortal music, ears open fresh here.
Do not refuse to sit again, play one more tune for me,
I shall compose for you this ballad, "Song of the Pipa," free.

Touched by my words, she stood a long time, lost in thought,
Returned to seat, tightened strings, tempo fiercely caught.
Melancholy unlike previous sounds, sad and low-borne,
Full hall hears again, covering faces, tears profuse.
Who among those seated shed most tears in silent grief?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, blue robe soaked, past relief.

低眉信手续续弹，说尽心中无限事。
轻拢慢捻抹复挑，初为霓裳后六幺。

嘈嘈切切错杂弹，大珠小珠落玉盘。
间关莺语花底滑，幽咽泉流冰下难。
冰泉冷涩弦凝绝，凝绝不通声暂歇。
别有幽愁暗恨生，此时无声胜有声。
银瓶乍破水浆迸，铁骑突出刀枪鸣。
曲终收拨当心画，四弦一声如裂帛。
东船西舫悄无言，唯见江心秋月白。
沉吟放拨插弦中，整顿衣裳起敛容。
自言本是京城女，家在虾蟆陵下住。
十三学得琵琶成，名属教坊第一部。
曲罢曾教善才服，妆成每被秋娘妒。
五陵年少争缠头，一曲红绡不知数。
钿头银篦击节碎，血色罗裙翻酒污。
今年欢笑复明年，秋月春风等闲度。
弟走从军阿姨死，暮去朝来颜色故。
门前冷落鞍马稀，老大嫁作商人妇。
商人重利轻别离，前月浮梁买茶去。
去来江口守空船，绕船月明江水寒。
夜深忽梦少年事，梦啼妆泪红阑干。
我闻琵琶已叹息，又闻此语重唧唧。
同是天涯沦落人，相逢何必曾相识！
我从去年辞帝京，谪居卧病浔阳城。
浔阳地僻无音乐，终岁不闻丝竹声。
住近湓江地低湿，黄芦苦竹绕宅生。
其间旦暮闻何物？杜鹃啼血猿哀鸣。
春江花朝秋月夜，往往取酒还独倾。
岂无山歌与村笛？呕哑嘲哳难为听。
今夜闻君琵琶语，如听仙乐耳暂明。
莫辞更坐弹一曲，为君翻作琵琶行。
感我此言良久立，却坐促弦弦转急。
凄凄不似向前声，满座重闻皆掩泣。
座中泣下谁最多？江州司马青衫湿。"}

By night I bid farewell to my guest by the banks of Xunyang;
Maple leaves and reed flowers rustle in the autumn chill.
I dismount, he steps aboard his boat, we raise our wine-cups high,
But no music plays to fill the air or lift our spirits sky.
Though drunk, joy remains elusive; sorrow looms before parting;
At separation’s hour, the moon sinks deep into the river’s mirroring.

Suddenly, from across the water, the pipa’s notes arise;
Host forgets to go home, guest delays to set out under skies.
Seeking the source, I ask softly who is playing so sweetly;
The pipa pauses, hesitant, as if words are locked tightly.
We move our boats close together, inviting her to appear;
More wine is poured, lamps re-lit, the banquet starts anew here.
After calling ten thousand times, she finally emerges shy,
Still holding her pipa close, half hiding face from eye.

She turns the pegs, plucks the strings, a few preliminary sounds;
Before the melody forms, emotion already abounds.
Each string suppresses sighs, each note conveys deep longing,
As if telling of a lifetime spent in unfulfilled yearning.
Eyes lowered, fingers move freely, strumming continuous lines,
Expressing all the infinite sorrows within her mind.
Light gathering, slow twisting, sweeping then picking once more,
First "Rainbow Garments" dances, then "Six Strings" on the floor.

The thick strings thunder loudly, like rain pouring down fast;
The thin strings whisper softly, voices hushed at last.
Loud and soft intertwined, they play in complex harmony,
Like pearls large and small falling onto a jade tray, vividly.
Melodious as orioles singing beneath bright flower blooms,
Choked and sobbing like spring waters trapped under ice’s glooms.
When the icy stream chokes cold, strings seem frozen and still,
Blocked and silent for a moment, breath held tight against will.

Hidden grief and secret resentments now begin to stir;
In this silence, sound speaks louder than any word ever were.
Then silver vases shatter suddenly, water bursts forth strong,
Iron cavalry charge forward, swords and spears clash along.
The song ends; she draws the plectrum across the center strings,
Four chords ring out sharply, tearing silk with violent springs.
Boats east and west fall silent, no one dares speak a word,
Only seeing the autumn moon shine white where river curved.

She hesitates, inserts the pick between the strings’ tension,
Straightens clothes, composes face, showing dignified repentance.
“I was born,” she says, “a girl of the imperial capital’s heart,
Living near the Toad Mound Hill, since childhood’s early start.
At thirteen, I mastered pipa art, fame reached far and wide,
Ranked first among the Imperial Music Academy’s pride.
After performances, even masters bowed to my skill’s grace,
My beauty made rival courtesans jealous in their place.
Young nobles from Five Tombs fought to offer me their gifts,
Red silk scarves piled high, counting countless shifts.
Gold-inlaid hairpins snapped when keeping time with beats,
Blood-red skirts stained with spilled wine, memories bittersweet.
Year after year of laughter passed, seasons flew away,
Autumn moons, spring breezes wasted carelessly by day.

Brother joined the army; auntie died; youth faded fast,
Dusk gave way to dawn, beauty vanished, shadows cast.
Front door grew desolate, horses rare, visitors few,
Old and weary, I married a merchant, bound to him too.
He values profit over love, cares little for goodbye,
Last month went to Fuliang town to buy tea, leaving dry.
Since he left, I guard an empty boat at river mouth alone,
Surrounded by clear moonlight, cold water flowing tone.
Deep in night, dreams return to days of girlish delight,
Waking tears stain rouge cheeks, running red through the night.”

Hearing the pipa, I had sighed deeply already sore,
Now these words add weight upon my chest, making grief more.
Both of us are exiled souls wandering ends of earth,
Meeting now, why need we know what happened before birth?

Since last year I left the capital, demoted and ill,
Stuck in Xunyang City, resting poor, quiet and still.
This remote place knows no music, silk sounds never reach,
All year long, ears starve for melodies beyond speech.
Living near Pen River, ground low and damp with mist,
Yellow reeds and bitter bamboo surround where I exist.
Morning and evening, what do I hear but cries of pain?
Cuckoos bleeding red voices, monkeys wailing in vain.
Spring rivers, flower mornings, autumn nights beneath moon’s glow,
Often take up wine alone, letting sorrow flow.
Are there no mountain songs or village pipes to cheer?
Crude and noisy sounds hard to bear, bringing fear.
Tonight hearing your pipa speech, celestial tones rise clear,
Like listening to immortal music, ears open fresh here.
Do not refuse to sit again, play one more tune for me,
I shall compose for you this ballad, "Song of the Pipa," free.

Touched by my words, she stood a long time, lost in thought,
Returned to seat, tightened strings, tempo fiercely caught.
Melancholy unlike previous sounds, sad and low-borne,
Full hall hears again, covering faces, tears profuse.
Who among those seated shed most tears in silent grief?
The Prefect of Jiangzhou, blue robe soaked, past relief."}

source.title: 黄鹤楼送孟浩然之广陵
source.author: 李白
source.text:
故人西辞黄鹤楼，烟花三月下扬州。
孤帆远影碧空尽，唯见长江天际流。
